title: memoryWrite reports SUCCESS after a swallowed disk-append failure — the entry lives only in RAM and vanishes on next launch
failureScenario: appendShardLine catches ANY fs.appendFileSync error and only records telemetry: `catch (err) { recordSwarmError('swarmMemory.persist.failed', err, ...) }` (633-637) — it never rethrows. persist() (640-642) returns void, and memoryWrite ignores it: after `persist(entry)` (574) it unconditionally does `entries.push(stored)` / `seenHashes.add` (582-583) and `return entry` (624). Concrete path: user is editing files, an antivirus/backup/Dropbox handle briefly locks <deviceId>.jsonl (routine on Windows — the repo even documents this race in contextPinStore.ts:94), OR the disk is momentarily full. Agent calls memory_write('decision: we chose Postgres over Mongo because X'). appendFileSync throws EBUSY/ENOSPC → swallowed. memory_write returns the entry with an id → the MCP tool reports success → the agent believes the decision is durably saved and moves on. The line never reached disk. Next launch, reloadFrom reads the shard, the decision is absent, and the agent re-litigates a settled decision. No user-visible error at any point.
whyItMatters: For a 'memory brain that must never silently lie to or lose data,' this is the core violation: the write API's success return is decoupled from durability. A single transient IO hiccup during normal operation silently drops exactly the high-value curated memory (decision/fact/result) the feature exists to preserve, and the agent is actively misled into thinking it was saved.
proposedFix: Make persistence failure observable to the caller. appendShardLine should return a boolean (or throw); persist() should propagate it; memoryWrite should either throw (so the MCP handler surfaces a real error to the agent) or attach a `durable:false` flag on the returned entry AND retry-on-next-flush. At minimum, do not add the entry to seenHashes when the append failed, so a later re-ingest/retry can re-attempt the write instead of the content-hash guard permanently masking the lost line.

verdict.evidence:
The full failure chain is real and reachable; every guard I looked for is absent. Quotes:

1) The swallow (swarmMemory.ts:629-638): `function appendShardLine(raw, ctx): void { if (!memPath) return; try { fs.appendFileSync(memPath, ...) } catch (err) { // ... Surface it. recordSwarmError('swarmMemory.persist.failed', err, { entryId: ctx }) } }`. It catches ANY error, never rethrows. `recordSwarmError` (telemetry.ts:171-193) only calls Sentry; line 177 `if (!Sentry) return` means when Sentry is unconfigured it does literally nothing. Either way the caller/agent never sees it — the "Surface it" comment surfaces only to backend telemetry.

2) No propagation (swarmMemory.ts:640-642): `function persist(entry): void { appendShardLine(JSON.stringify(entry), entry.id) }` — returns void.

3) memoryWrite ignores it (swarmMemory.ts:574,582-583,624): `persist(entry)` then unconditionally `entries.push(stored)`, `if (stored.hash) seenHashes.add(stored.hash)`, and `return entry`. No check of persistence outcome; entry is added to the in-RAM dedup guard even though it never hit disk.

4) Caller reports SUCCESS (index.ts:1769-1784): the MCP handler `memoryWrite` does `const e = await memoryWrite({...}); recordMetric({ t:'write', ok:true, ...}); return e` and only throws in a catch that is never entered (memoryWrite swallowed the error). mcpServer.ts:577-582 then returns `result:{ content:[{type:'text', text:JSON.stringify(result)}] }` with NO isError — the agent gets the entry (id/ts/hash) as an unambiguous success. The isError path (583-592) requires a throw, which does not happen.

5) Vanishes next launch (swarmMemory.ts:188-210): `reloadFrom` does `entries.length=0; seenHashes.clear()`, reads ONLY `fs.readFileSync(p)` per shard, and rebuilds `seenHashes` from what is on disk (line 210 `if (e.hash) seenHashes.add(e.hash)`). A line that never reached disk is absent from both `entries` and `seenHashes`.

6) No recovery path exists. Searched every `writeFileSync(memPath,...)` / snapshot / flush: `rewriteSelfShard` (1457-1468) reads from disk so a lost line stays lost; the only from-memory full rewrite is `setSyncDir(null)`'s off-toggle to legacyPath (1511-1514), a rare admin action, not routine. `before-quit` (index.ts:2204-2212) does NOT flush memory. The periodic indexer (memoryIndexer.ts) only runs ingest runners that append via memoryWrite; it never re-persists existing in-RAM `entries`.

7) The environmental trigger is real and acknowledged in this very repo: contextPinStore.ts:91-98 `catch { // Windows: rename can race with antivirus / briefly held handles. Fall back to overwrite in place ... }` — the same Windows AV/held-handle race the finding cites, and there they added a fallback. appendShardLine has NO such fallback. The product also encourages putting the shard in a cloud-synced folder (setSyncDir), which raises concurrent-lock/EBUSY likelihood; ENOSPC is likewise real. The tool contract explicitly promises durability (mcpServer.ts:263: "shared persistent memory ... Anything stored here can be recalled later"), so a false success signal directly violates the advertised contract.
verdict.notes:
Adversarial verdict: I tried to refute and could not — no retry, no propagation, no quit/periodic flush, no read-back check; all callers propagate success. Location cited (swarmMemory.ts:633) and mechanism are accurate. Severity high is appropriate: silent, agent-invisible loss on the core value-prop path, with an affirmatively-wrong success signal, under realistic Windows-lock / cloud-sync / disk-full triggers.

One minor overstatement in the finding's PROPOSED-FIX rationale (not the core claim): "the content-hash guard permanently masking the lost line." seenHashes is per-session and is rebuilt from disk on next launch (swarmMemory.ts:190,210), so an INGESTION-derived write whose source transcript/file still exists WOULD be re-attempted on next launch via the hasHash-gated re-ingest — i.e. self-healing. The permanent-loss case is a DIRECT agent memory_write of NOVEL content with no backing source file — which is exactly the finding's headline scenario and concrete example ("decision: we chose Postgres over Mongo"). So the primary finding (title, location, failure scenario, severity) is CONFIRMED in full; only the word "permanently" in the fix rationale is scope-narrowed to direct novel writes. This nuance does not reduce the core severity.

title: Init failure sets memPath=null for the WHOLE session — every subsequent write is silently discarded while memory_write still returns success
failureScenario: initSwarmMemory wraps mkdirSync(syncDir)/copyFileSync/writeFileSync/reloadFrom in one try; on ANY throw it does `recordSwarmError(...); memPath = null` (277-278). The most reachable trigger: cross-machine sync is enabled and the sync folder is a cloud/network path (Dropbox/OneDrive/SMB) that is offline or not-yet-mounted at launch → `fs.mkdirSync(syncDir, { recursive: true })` (253) throws → memPath=null. There is no retry and no other code path ever re-assigns memPath (only 254/269/278 and setSyncDir). For the rest of the session: appendShardLine's `if (!memPath) return` (630) makes persist() a no-op, memoryClear's `if (!memPath) return` (1248) makes clear a no-op, yet memoryWrite still embeds, pushes to `entries`, and returns the entry as success (582/624). The user works a full session; ingest + reflection + manual memory_write all appear to succeed; the entire session's memory is RAM-only and is gone on the next launch. The only signal is one telemetry event the user never sees.
whyItMatters: A momentary folder-unavailable at startup (extremely common with cloud-synced folders and laptops resuming from sleep) permanently poisons the whole session into silent data-loss mode, with the API continuing to report every write as successful. This is the archetypal 'silently fail and continue' failure the audit targets, at the worst possible scope (all writes, whole session).
proposedFix: On init failure, fall back to the local legacyPath as a writable target instead of nulling memPath (so writes still persist somewhere), and expose a durable 'memory is read-only / degraded' state through getSyncStatus() so the UI can warn the user. Additionally, attempt a lazy re-init on the first write after failure (retry mkdir/open) rather than giving up for the entire process lifetime.

verdict.evidence:
Every specific claim in the finding is code-accurate at the cited lines; refutation attempts all failed.

1) Init nulls memPath for the whole session on ANY throw. swarmMemory.ts:251-278:
```
251  try {
252    if (syncDir) {
253      fs.mkdirSync(syncDir, { recursive: true })
254      memPath = path.join(syncDir, `${deviceId}.jsonl`)
...
267      reloadFrom(shardFiles())
...
273  } catch (err) {
277    recordSwarmError('swarmMemory.init.failed', err, { memPath })
278    memPath = null
279  }
```
The mkdirSync at 253 is the reachable trigger for a sync folder that is offline/unmounted at launch (network share / VPN not yet up / cloud daemon starting). copyFileSync(259)/writeFileSync(261)/reloadFrom(267) are additional throw sites that also land at 278.

2) No retry, no re-init, no local fallback. grep of memPath assignments across the file: 254, 269, 278 (=null), 284 (test-only). The only recovery is setSyncDir (1506-1519), which requires manual user action. There is no write-path re-init.

3) Writes silently discarded while memory_write returns success. memoryWrite (swarmMemory.ts:531-624) has no memPath guard — only `if (!input || ... !input.content.trim()) throw` at 532-534. It runs embed, then persist(entry) at 574, then `entries.push(stored)` at 582, then `return entry` at 624. persist→appendShardLine no-ops:
```
629  function appendShardLine(raw: string, ctx: string): void {
630    if (!memPath) return
```
So the entry is returned as success but never written to disk.

4) memoryClear disk step is skipped: swarmMemory.ts:1248 `if (!memPath) return` (in-memory wipe at 1240-1247 still runs; only the disk tombstone/truncate is skipped — a minor imprecision in the finding, immaterial to durability).

5) No user-facing degraded signal. syncDir is set at line 240 BEFORE the try and is never nulled in the catch, so getSyncStatus (1397-1411) still returns `syncing: !!syncDir` (=true), `dir: syncDir`, `count: entries.length` (a growing RAM count) — a healthy-looking status with no memPath/degraded field. The only status IPC is memory:sync-status → getSyncStatus (index.ts:1290-1291). The only failure signal is the telemetry event at swarmMemory.ts:277.

6) Reachable in production. index.ts:1884 `initSwarmMemory(app.getPath('userData'))` (no opts) → swarmMemory.ts:240 `syncDir = ... readSyncConfig(resolved)` loads the persisted sync dir. Users enable sync via the folder picker (index.ts:1299-1307 → setSyncDir → writeSyncConfig), so on the next launch with the folder offline, 253 throws and 278 nulls memPath for the session.

Net effect: only THIS session's new writes (ingest + reflection + manual memory_write) are lost — they existed only in RAM; prior memories in the shard files survive and reload once the folder is back online. That matches the finding ("the entire session's memory is RAM-only and is gone on the next launch").
verdict.notes: Severity kept at high. The bug is gated behind a non-default precondition — cross-machine sync enabled AND the target offline/unwritable specifically at launch — so local-only (default) users are unaffected (else-branch at 269-271 writes to local userData, which essentially never fails). But the finding states that precondition explicitly and does not overclaim. When the condition is met, the outcome is silent, total loss of the session's memory with affirmative false-success (memory_write returns the entry; getSyncStatus reports syncing:true with a healthy count) and no retry/fallback/warning. For a data-durability defect, silent loss with false success warrants high regardless of the affected subpopulation. The proposed fix (fall back to legacyPath on init failure, expose a degraded state via getSyncStatus, and lazy-retry re-init on first write) is sound and directly addresses the three confirmed gaps.

title: A crash mid-append leaves an unterminated line that silently swallows the NEXT good write (no JSONL frame repair on init)
failureScenario:
Lines are framed by a trailing '
' appended AFTER the payload: `fs.appendFileSync(memPath, (encKey ? encryptLine(encKey, raw) : raw) + '
')` (632). Entries can be ~24 KB (up to 16 KB content + a serialized 384-float embedding), so a write spans several filesystem pages. If the process is SIGKILLed / force-quit / OOM-killed / loses power partway through the append (writeFileSync loops over multiple write() syscalls), the shard ends with a truncated line and NO newline, e.g. `...{"id":"mem-A","content":"foo`. On relaunch reloadFrom does `raw.split('
')` (199) and parseShardLine JSON.parses each; the truncated tail fails and is skipped (169) — fine so far. But memPath is now set to that file, and the NEXT memoryWrite appends at EOF (O_APPEND): the bytes become `...foo{"id":"mem-B",...}
`, i.e. mem-B is now on the SAME physical line as the truncated mem-A. On the following reload, split('
') yields one line `...foo{"id":"mem-B",...}` which fails JSON.parse and is skipped — so mem-B (a perfectly good, fully-written memory) is silently lost too. init never checks/repairs the trailing-newline frame (local branch 270-271, sync seed 257-263 via copyFileSync preserve whatever framing exists).
whyItMatters: The 'killed mid-write' case the audit calls out doesn't just lose the torn entry — it corrupts the frame so that the first healthy write after recovery is also destroyed, and both losses are completely silent. Append-only durability is the store's whole safety story, and unguarded line framing quietly breaks it.
proposedFix:
Guarantee frame integrity on open: in initSwarmMemory, if the shard is non-empty and its last byte is not '
', append a single '
' (or truncate the trailing partial line) before any new append. Cheaper alternative: have appendShardLine stat/seek and write a leading '
' when the file doesn't already end in one. This makes a torn tail cost at most the torn entry, never a subsequent one.

verdict.evidence:
The CODE MECHANISM is accurate and unguarded — I cannot refute it — but the SEVERITY ("high") and the failure-trigger list are overstated, so PARTIAL.

CONFIRMED (code is exactly as described, no missed guard):
- swarmMemory.ts:632 `fs.appendFileSync(memPath, (encKey ? encryptLine(encKey, raw) : raw) + '\n')` — the '\n' is a TRAILING terminator, there is NO fsync, and no options arg (default flag 'a' → append at EOF). So a file that ends without '\n' will have the next payload concatenated onto its last line.
- appendShardLine (629-638) does NOT stat/seek/check for a trailing '\n' before appending: `function appendShardLine(raw, ctx){ if(!memPath) return; try{ fs.appendFileSync(...) } ... }`.
- initSwarmMemory (230-272) performs NO frame repair on either path — sync: `fs.copyFileSync(legacyPath, memPath)` (259) / `fs.writeFileSync(memPath,'')` (261); local: `if (fs.existsSync(memPath)) reloadFrom([memPath])` (270) `else fs.writeFileSync(memPath,'')` (271). The auditor's "init never checks/repairs the trailing-newline frame" is TRUE.
- reloadFrom:199 `for (const line of raw.split('\n')) parseShardLine(line, adds)` + parseShardLine:169 `try { obj = JSON.parse(plain) } catch { return /* skip malformed line */ }` — a merged `...foo{"id":"mem-B",...}` line fails JSON.parse and is silently dropped. So the good next write IS lost on the following reload.
- localEmbedder.ts:26 `export const EMBED_DIM = 384` + memoryWrite:569-574 attaches the embedding then persists the full entry, so entries are ~24 KB (16 KB MAX_CONTENT + serialized 384-float array) = multi-block, making a partial-block torn write physically possible.
- Grep of src/: NO fsync/flushSync/writeSync anywhere — no durability barrier prevents the torn/unflushed tail. The same no-fsync append+'\n' pattern is codebase-wide (memoryGraph.ts:214, metricsLedger.ts:189, etc.). rewriteSelfShard (1457-1469) would re-frame on '\n' but only runs on encryption enable/disable, never on init, and would NOT re-split an already-merged JSON line anyway. No test covers torn-line/frame behavior. So nothing refutes the mechanism.

WHY IT IS NARROWER / LESS SEVERE THAN "high":
1. Triggers overstated. The finding headlines "SIGKILLed / force-quit / OOM-killed" — these do NOT tear a ~24 KB local-FS regular-file write. appendFileSync issues a single write(2) that copies the whole '\n'-terminated buffer into the page cache in one call (24 KB never returns a short count on a local FS, so the writeFileSync loop runs once — there is no inter-syscall window). The page cache SURVIVES process death and the OS flushes the complete line. Only power loss / OS crash / kernel panic (page cache lost before writeback, ~seconds) can leave a torn OR null-padded tail. So 3 of the 4 enumerated causes are inert on a typical local store; the bug is power-loss-gated. (Niche caveat: a syncDir on a network mount could revive the process-kill vector via short writes — atypical config.)
2. Blast radius = exactly ONE entry. Only the first write after the torn tail is swallowed; every later write carries its own trailing '\n' and parses fine (mem-C, mem-D... self-frame). Not cascading — the finding's own title correctly says "the NEXT good write" (singular), which is narrower than a "high" would imply.
3. In-session survival. The sacrificed entry is pushed to the in-memory `entries` at write time (582) and is fully usable for the entire session it is written in; loss only manifests on a SUBSEQUENT relaunch.
4. Self-healing for the bulk. Ingested message/code chunks (the dominant content) are re-written by the every-launch re-indexer — comment at 399-401 "the auto-indexer re-runs ingest every launch, so the tags re-derive for free each session"; the lost entry's hash is no longer in seenHashes (547/583), so re-ingest re-adds it. Only a directly agent-authored, non-re-ingestable decision/fact/note is PERMANENTLY lost.
5. Requires a 3-event intersection: (a) a power-loss/panic torn write, (b) ≥1 more write in the next session, (c) another relaunch.

Net: a real, silent, single-entry durability corner-case gated on a hardware-level crash — genuine and worth the cheap init-time frame check the auditor proposes, but "low" (medium at most, given the silence) rather than "high," and reachable only via power loss/panic, not the process kills it leads with.
verdict.notes: Same unterminated-frame exposure exists in the sibling JSONL logs written the identical way (memoryGraph.ts:214 edges, metricsLedger.ts:189, mnemeCompetence.ts:45, mnemeIdentity.ts:56, agentEventBus.ts:159) — none fsync or repair framing — so if this is fixed it should be fixed as a shared appendShardLine-style helper. The proposed fix (init: if last byte != '\n' append one; or appendShardLine writes a leading '\n' when the file doesn't end in one) is sound and would cap a torn tail's cost at the torn entry alone.

title: Whole-shard rewrite for encryption enable/disable is non-atomic — an interrupted rewrite truncates or corrupts the entire device shard
failureScenario: rewriteSelfShard reads the whole shard into memory, transforms every line, then rewrites in place with `fs.writeFileSync(memPath, out.length ? out.join('\n') + '\n' : '')` (1468) — no temp-file+rename, unlike the repo's own atomicWriteJson (agentMcpRegistry.ts:29) and contextPinStore.ts:88-92. writeFileSync opens with 'w', which TRUNCATES the file first and then streams the (potentially many-MB) buffer. If the process crashes / loses power / hits ENOSPC after truncation but before the full buffer is flushed, the shard is left empty or half-written — and the write error is swallowed (`catch { /* best effort */ }`, 1468). This path runs during setSyncPassphrase (enable encryption / unlock a new device, 1487) and disableSyncEncryption (1496): a user with a large synced brain turns encryption on, the machine is put to sleep / force-quit mid-rewrite, and their entire device shard is now truncated. Because each device only writes its own shard, that content isn't recoverable from peers if they haven't synced it.
whyItMatters: This converts a routine settings toggle into a whole-shard wipe on any ill-timed interruption. The codebase already has the atomic-write primitive; the memory brain — the one store where loss is unacceptable — is the one that skips it.
proposedFix: Rewrite via temp-file + fsync + atomic rename (reuse the atomicWriteJson pattern): write to memPath+'.tmp', fsync it, then renameSync over memPath, with the contextPinStore Windows fallback. Do not swallow the write error — surface it and keep the original file intact on failure.

verdict.evidence:
Every mechanical claim in the finding is verified against the real code; nothing guards this path.

1) The non-atomic in-place rewrite with swallowed error is exactly as described — swarmMemory.ts:1457-1468:
```
function rewriteSelfShard(xform: (plain: string) => string): void {
  if (!memPath) return
  let raw: string
  try { raw = fs.readFileSync(memPath, 'utf8') } catch { return }
  const out: string[] = []
  for (const line of raw.split('\n')) { ... out.push(plain === null ? s : xform(plain)) }
  try { fs.writeFileSync(memPath, out.length ? out.join('\n') + '\n' : '') } catch { /* best effort */ }
}
```
`fs.writeFileSync(path, string)` opens with flag 'w' (O_CREAT|O_TRUNC) — it truncates the shard to 0 bytes, then streams the buffer. A crash/power-loss/ENOSPC after truncation leaves the file empty or partial, and the throw is silently swallowed.

2) memPath is this device's own shard, not a shared/derived file — swarmMemory.ts:254 `memPath = path.join(syncDir, `${deviceId}.jsonl`)`. Normal writes only ever APPEND to it (line 632 `fs.appendFileSync(memPath, ...)`), and rewriteSelfShard is the only full-rewrite of it. So the shard is the accumulation of all of this device's memory writes and each device writes only its own shard — confirming the finding's "not recoverable from peers" claim (a local truncation propagates through the cloud provider; a peer only has an independent copy if it synced before the truncation).

3) The buffer really can be multi-MB: persisted lines are full JSON entries including the 384-dim embedding (serializeEntry, swarmMemory.ts:777-782 emits `{ ...e, embedding: Array.from(v) }`; entries carry `.embedding`, ~6-8 KB/line), so an active brain of thousands of entries is tens of MB — a wide partial-write window.

4) No in-memory recovery: after the rewrite, both callers call reloadFrom(shardFiles()) which wipes state and RE-READS disk (swarmMemory.ts:188-199 `entries.length = 0 ... raw = fs.readFileSync(p) ... parseShardLine`). The pre-crash in-memory union is discarded; on restart the truncated shard is authoritative.

5) Reachable from user-facing IPC. Callers: setSyncPassphrase (swarmMemory.ts:1487 `rewriteSelfShard((plain) => encryptLine(key, plain))`) and disableSyncEncryption (1496 `rewriteSelfShard((plain) => plain)`). Both are thin-wrapped IPC handlers with no backup/guard — index.ts:1314-1320 `ipcMain.handle('memory:set-sync-passphrase', ... setSyncPassphrase(...))` and `ipcMain.handle('memory:disable-sync-encryption', ... disableSyncEncryption())`. Toggling at-rest encryption in settings hits this directly.

6) The repo demonstrably knows the atomic pattern and uses it for LESS critical data — agentMcpRegistry.ts:29-33 `atomicWriteJson` (`writeFileSync(tmp,...); renameSync(tmp, path)`) and contextPinStore.ts:86-98 `writeAll` (temp + renameSync + Windows overwrite fallback). rewriteSelfShard is the inconsistent outlier.

Severity stays high — and the trigger is actually BROADER than the finding argues: ENOSPC needs no crash at all. On a full disk, writeFileSync truncates the shard to 0, the write fails, the catch swallows it, and setSyncPassphrase still caches encKey and returns getSyncStatus() reporting success — silent, unrecoverable loss of the device's unique memories while telling the user encryption is on. Given permanent data loss, a swallowed error, a false-success return, and no backup, high is justified; the proposed temp-file+fsync+rename fix (already the repo's pattern) is correct.

Minor wording nuance only (does not lower severity): in the half-written subcase, JSONL is line-oriented so earlier fully-written lines survive and only the tail is lost — "corrupts the ENTIRE shard" is literally true only in the empty-file/ENOSPC case; otherwise it is tail-loss up to total.
verdict.notes: Adversarial attempt to refute failed: memPath is non-null on this path (setSyncPassphrase throws if !syncDir, swarmMemory.ts:1476, and syncDir implies memPath is set at 254); the error is genuinely swallowed (contrast appendShardLine at 633-636 which calls recordSwarmError); reloadFrom re-reads disk so there is no in-memory heal; and the atomic-write helpers the auditor cited exist verbatim. All six load-bearing claims confirmed. Only refinement: the ENOSPC (full-disk) path makes this reachable without any crash, which if anything strengthens the finding.

title: Turning cross-machine sync OFF silently discards all reinforcement-learning (usage) counts and can revert to a stale/empty local store
failureScenario: setSyncDir(null) snapshots the unioned memories into legacyPath with `const snap = entries.map(serializeEntry).join('\n'); fs.writeFileSync(legacyPath, snap ? snap + '\n' : '')` (1513-1514), then re-inits local-only. Two durability defects: (1) serializeEntry (777-782) emits ONLY MemoryEntry objects — it does NOT emit the `{reinforce:[...]}` delta control lines. usageMap is rebuilt exclusively from those delta lines on reload (reloadFrom 219-227, replaying pendingReinforce). So after the toggle, usageMap is empty: every BB13/BB14 usage/'helpful' signal the fleet accumulated is permanently gone, and ranking (learnedUtility uses `useCount`, 983) regresses — memories the user repeatedly confirmed helpful lose their learned boost. (2) The snapshot writeFileSync is non-atomic and its failure is swallowed (`catch { /* best effort */ }`, 1515). If it throws (disk full, or OOM building a multi-GB join() string over a large synced brain), legacyPath is left as a STALE pre-sync file (or empty), then initSwarmMemory(local) loads that — so turning sync off can silently revert the brain to an ancient snapshot and drop everything accumulated while sync was on.
whyItMatters: A reversible-looking UI action (stop syncing) silently and permanently erases the learning layer and, on any write hiccup, most of the store — with no error surfaced. That is exactly 'regress/drift its learning' plus silent data-loss.
proposedFix: When snapshotting for sync-off, also serialize the current usageMap as `{reinforce:[...]}` lines (and any live tombstones/clearEpoch) into legacyPath so learning survives the round-trip. Write the snapshot atomically (temp+fsync+rename) and, if it fails, ABORT the switch (do not overwrite the sync config / re-init) so the user isn't dropped onto a stale local store.

verdict.evidence:
Both defects are real, correctly located, and reachable through a normal one-click UI action. My adversarial counter-hypotheses all failed against the code.

REACHABILITY (full chain to setSyncDir(null)):
- Memory.tsx:282 button "Turn off sync (keep memory local)" -> Memory.tsx:59-62 `disableSync` -> `await window.termpolis.memorySetSyncDir(null)`
- preload/index.ts:153 `memorySetSyncDir: (dir) => ipcRenderer.invoke('memory:set-sync-dir', { dir })`
- index.ts:1294-1295 `ipcMain.handle('memory:set-sync-dir', ... => setSyncDir(opts?.dir ?? null))` -> setSyncDir(null)
- The UI even reports it as benign: Memory.tsx:65 `'Sync turned off — memory is now local to this machine.'`

DEFECT 1 — usage counts silently dropped (unconditional, every sync-off):
- swarmMemory.ts:1511-1516 (snapshot branch, exactly as cited): `const snap = entries.map(serializeEntry).join('\n'); fs.writeFileSync(legacyPath, snap ? snap + '\n' : '')`
- serializeEntry (777-782) emits ONLY a MemoryEntry: `return JSON.stringify(v ? { ...e, embedding: ... } : e)` — no `{reinforce}` control lines.
- MemoryEntry interface (31-48) has NO useCount field, so the entry itself cannot carry a usage count. (Refutes "the snapshot preserves useCount on the entry.")
- usageMap's ONLY persistence is `{reinforce}` delta lines: comment 351-354 "Persisted as additive CRDT-safe DELTA control lines `{reinforce:[{id,used,ts}]}` in the shard and replayed on reload"; parseShardLine 173-181 pushes them into pendingReinforce; there is no separate usageMap file (grep of the module confirms none). (Refutes "a separate usageMap store survives.")
- reloadFrom 219-227 rebuilds usageMap EXCLUSIVELY from pendingReinforce: `usageMap.clear(); if (pendingReinforce.length > 0) { ... usageMap.set(r.id, ...) }`. Snapshot->legacyPath has no reinforce lines, so on setSyncDir->initSwarmMemory->reloadFrom([legacyPath]) (270 `if (fs.existsSync(memPath)) reloadFrom([memPath])`, memPath=legacyPath at 269) usageMap ends up empty.
- Ranking regresses BY DEFAULT (refutes "useCount is gated off"): swarmMemory.ts:983 passes `useCount: usageMap.get(r.id) ?? 0` into learnedUtility on the main search path; mnemeRetrieval.ts:65-78 applies it unconditionally with NON-ZERO defaults LEARNED_UTILITY_DEFAULTS.usageWeight=0.05, usageCap=0.2 (44-46): `usageNudge = min(0.2, 0.05*ln(1+useCount)); return relevance*(1+importanceNudge)*(1+usageNudge)` — up to +20% boost lost. Unlike graphFusion/adapt/prf (default OFF), the usage nudge is live.

DEFECT 2 — swallowed non-atomic write reverts to a stale/empty store (conditional on a write failure):
- swarmMemory.ts:1515 the write's failure is swallowed: `} catch { /* best effort */ }`, then execution proceeds unconditionally to 1517 `writeSyncConfig(userDataDir, clean)` and 1518 `initSwarmMemory(userDataDir, { syncDir: clean })`, which loads legacyPath (270).
- legacyPath is frozen at sync-enable time: enabling sync copies it into the device shard once (257-263 `if (!fs.existsSync(memPath)) { ... fs.copyFileSync(legacyPath, memPath) }`) but never rewrites legacyPath; during sync-on all appends go to the shard (appendShardLine 629-632 writes memPath = syncDir shard). So a failed snapshot leaves legacyPath as the OLD pre-sync content -> the active brain silently reverts to that stale snapshot, dropping ALL content accumulated while sync was on (not just usage counts).
verdict.notes:
Verdict CONFIRMED; I kept severity at high but with two honest scope caveats the finding slightly overstates:

1) "permanently gone" is a mild overstatement. The `{reinforce}` delta lines still physically exist in the per-device shard files in the (now de-referenced) sync folder; re-pointing sync at the same folder would replay them (initSwarmMemory won't re-migrate since the shard exists, but reloadFrom(shardFiles()) re-reads every shard and rebuilds usageMap). BUT setSyncDir writes `{dir:null}` (writeSyncConfig) so the app discards the folder pointer and gives no hint, and local-only mode never reads it again — so from the active store's perspective it is effectively lost. Not a refutation.

2) Impact splits into two tiers. The UNCONDITIONAL consequence (every sync-off) is a ranking-quality regression only — the usage nudge is capped at +20%, memory CONTENT is preserved — which on its own is ~medium. The CATASTROPHIC consequence (defect 2: full revert of the active store to the stale pre-sync snapshot, losing all content added during sync) is high-impact but CONDITIONAL on fs.writeFileSync throwing. The finding's "OOM building a multi-GB join() string" trigger is speculative, but ordinary triggers (disk full, read-only/unavailable volume, permissions) are plausible and suffice. Net: high is justified because a one-click action advertised as safe ("keep memory local") silently discards fleet-accumulated reinforcement learning and, on any write failure, silently rolls the brain back to an old snapshot with the error swallowed.

The proposed fix is correct and appropriate: also serialize the live usageMap as `{reinforce}` lines (plus tombstones/clearEpoch) into the snapshot, write atomically (temp+fsync+rename), and abort the switch (skip writeSyncConfig/initSwarmMemory) if the snapshot fails rather than dropping the user onto a stale legacyPath.

title: loadOrCreateSalt regenerates and OVERWRITES the encryption salt on any transient read failure or corruption — permanently locking out all encrypted memory
failureScenario: The salt is critical key material (deriveKey = scryptSync(passphrase, salt), memoryCrypto.ts:28-30). loadOrCreateSalt tries to read it, and on ANY exception OR any non-16-byte result falls through to `const s = newSalt(); fs.writeFileSync(p, s.toString('base64'))` (1440-1441) — it OVERWRITES the existing salt file in the synced folder. The salt lives in the sync folder (SALT_FILE, 125). Reachable: user re-enters their (correct) passphrase via setSyncPassphrase (1478 calls loadOrCreateSalt) while the cloud-synced .termpolis-salt is momentarily unavailable, half-synced (wrong length), or corrupted by a bad merge → a brand-new salt is generated and written over the real one. deriveKey now yields a different key. If a peer's ciphertext happens to be present, findAnyEncryptedLine+decrypt fails → the user is told 'Incorrect passphrase for the existing encrypted memory' (1482) despite typing the right one; if no peer ciphertext is present yet, the new key is silently cached and this device re-encrypts under it — and every peer's existing ciphertext (encrypted under the original salt) becomes permanently undecryptable once the overwritten salt propagates.
whyItMatters: A transient unavailability or single-byte corruption of a non-secret helper file destroys the one piece of material needed to ever read the encrypted store again, and the failure masquerades as a wrong-passphrase error. That is silent, irreversible loss of the entire encrypted brain.
proposedFix: Only create a salt when the file genuinely does not exist (fs.existsSync === false). If the salt file exists but is unreadable or malformed, THROW/abort (surface 'memory salt unavailable, retry') instead of minting and writing a replacement — never overwrite an existing salt. Optionally keep a local backup copy of the salt in userData and cross-check before regenerating.

verdict.notes: Severity kept at high (not raised to critical) because, although the impact is silent, permanent, unrecoverable loss of all encrypted swarm memory, the trigger requires a transient/corrupt salt read to coincide with a passphrase-entry action. That coincidence is realistic for cloud-synced folders but not guaranteed on every invocation. It is a genuine, reachable data-destruction bug via a normal user flow — not a misread and not otherwise guarded.

title: Corrupt/undecryptable JSONL lines are skipped silently with no count or telemetry — partial shard corruption deletes memories invisibly
failureScenario: parseShardLine does `try { obj = JSON.parse(plain) } catch { return /* skip malformed line */ }` (169) with no counter and no telemetry, and reloadFrom (188-228) never tallies how many lines failed. Scenario: a shard file is partially corrupted — a bad three-way sync/merge of <deviceId>.jsonl, disk bit-rot, an editor that re-saved with a different encoding/BOM, or the torn-line merge from finding #3 — mangling, say, 5,000 of 200,000 lines. On next launch those 5,000 memories simply don't load. memoryStats()/getSyncStatus().count report the lower number as if that were the truth; nothing logs that anything was dropped. The user has no way to know their brain quietly shrank, and no signal to restore from a backup before the good copy is overwritten by the next rewrite.
whyItMatters: Silent, uncounted skipping of unparseable lines means on-disk corruption is indistinguishable from 'nothing was there,' defeating any chance of detection or recovery — the exact 'swallow and continue' pattern flagged as a solidity failure.
proposedFix: Count parse failures (and encrypted-but-undecryptable lines separately) in reloadFrom; when the count is non-zero, recordSwarmError with the file and tally, and expose a `corruptLinesSkipped` field on getSyncStatus()/memoryStats() so the UI can warn. Consider quarantining the corrupt shard (copy to .corrupt) before any subsequent rewrite so the raw bytes remain recoverable.

verdict.evidence:
CORE CLAIM CONFIRMED (plaintext path). swarmMemory.ts:169 is verbatim as quoted: `try { obj = JSON.parse(plain) } catch { return /* skip malformed line */ }` — no counter, no telemetry. reloadFrom (188-228) drives it with `for (const line of raw.split('\n')) parseShardLine(line, adds)` (199); parseShardLine returns void, so no failure count can propagate. memoryStats() returns `{ count: entries.length, capacity: maxEntries }` (418-419) and getSyncStatus() returns `count: entries.length` (1407) — no corruptLinesSkipped field. The only recordSwarmError sites are `swarmMemory.init.failed` (277) and `swarmMemory.persist.failed` (636); neither fires on a parse-skip. So for a PLAINTEXT store (the default — encKey is null until the user opts in via setSyncPassphrase), a corrupt line is dropped 100% silently and the count silently shrinks. That much is real and reachable.

OVERSTATEMENT 1 — "undecryptable lines ... no count or telemetry" is inaccurate for the ENCRYPTED case. Line 163-165: `if (isEncryptedLine(s)) { const dec = encKey ? decryptLine(encKey, s) : null; if (dec === null) { lockedShards = true; return } }`. memoryCrypto.ts:47-59 confirms decryptLine returns null on corruption/wrong-key (catch→null, no crash). That null sets `lockedShards`, which IS surfaced: SyncStatus has `locked: boolean` (1388) and getSyncStatus returns `locked: lockedShards` (1409). So an undecryptable/bit-rotted encrypted line produces a real (if coarse, boolean, semantically-"needs passphrase") signal — it is NOT "skipped silently with no telemetry." The finding conflates the plaintext path (truly silent) with the encrypted path (signaled).

OVERSTATEMENT 2 — "before the good copy is overwritten by the next rewrite" is largely false. The normal write path is append-only: appendShardLine uses `fs.appendFileSync(memPath, ...)` (629-638) — it never rewrites existing bytes, so corrupt lines that failed to parse remain on disk. The only shard-rewrite path, rewriteSelfShard (1457-1468), explicitly PRESERVES lines it can't handle: `out.push(plain === null ? s : xform(plain))` (1466) with the comment "Lines we can't decrypt are kept verbatim (never dropped)" (1456) — it iterates raw file lines, not the parsed in-memory `entries`, so it does not drop malformed/undecryptable lines either. The only truncation is an explicit user memoryClear() in local-only mode (`fs.writeFileSync(memPath, '')`, 1255); in sync mode even clear is a tombstone append (1252-1253). So the raw bytes generally survive and are recoverable — the true defect is "no signal telling the user to go look," not "the good copy gets overwritten."
verdict.notes:
Net: the finding is real but narrower/less severe than framed, hence PARTIAL. The genuine, actionable defect is an OBSERVABILITY gap on the plaintext path: parseShardLine (169) drops JSON.parse failures with no tally, reloadFrom (188-228) never counts them, and neither memoryStats() (418) nor getSyncStatus() (1397) exposes a corrupt-line count — so an externally-corrupted plaintext shard makes the brain shrink with zero user-facing signal. The proposed fix (count failures, recordSwarmError, expose corruptLinesSkipped) is reasonable.

Corrected to LOW because: (1) it is an observability gap, not a data-corruption bug — the code does not create the corruption, it under-reports pre-existing external corruption; (2) the encrypted path already surfaces a signal via getSyncStatus().locked (1409), contradicting the blanket "no telemetry" claim; (3) the raw bytes are not destroyed in normal operation — writes are append-only (632) and the only shard rewrite (rewriteSelfShard, 1466) preserves unparseable/undecryptable lines verbatim, so "deletes memories invisibly ... before the good copy is overwritten" overstates the permanence (recovery from the raw file is possible; a separate external event like a sync-provider file replacement or an explicit user clear would be needed for true loss). This silent-skip-a-corrupt-line pattern is a deliberate, codebase-wide convention (memoryGraph.ts:179, metricsLedger.ts:172, mnemeCompetence.ts:30, mnemeIdentity.ts:78), so the swarmMemory instance is not an anomalous oversight.

title: Appends are never fsync'd — memory_write acknowledges data that a power loss then discards
failureScenario: appendShardLine relies solely on `fs.appendFileSync(...)` (632), which opens/writes/closes but performs NO fsync/fdatasync — the bytes land in the OS page cache and are flushed lazily. memoryWrite returns success the instant appendFileSync returns. If the machine loses power (or the OS crashes / battery dies) within the flush window, the most recently 'saved' memories — potentially the entire last burst written by the 90s/30-min ingest passes or a series of manual memory_write calls — are gone even though every call reported success and no error was recorded anywhere. Because the id/hash was already admitted to seenHashes in RAM, nothing re-drives those specific writes either.
whyItMatters: The store's durability contract is 'append-only, retains everything written,' but without fsync a write is acknowledged before it is durable, so a crash silently rolls back confirmed memories. For a product whose thesis is never silently losing data, acknowledged-but-not-durable is a real gap.
proposedFix: For high-value writes (decision/fact/result and control lines), open the shard with an explicit fd, appendFileSync, then fs.fsyncSync(fd) before returning success (batch/debounce the fsync for bulk message-chunk ingest to bound cost). Combine with the frame-repair fix (finding #3) so a crash costs at most the un-fsync'd tail and never a subsequent entry.

verdict.evidence:
MECHANISM IS REAL (cannot refute): swarmMemory.ts:632 `fs.appendFileSync(memPath, (encKey ? encryptLine(encKey, raw) : raw) + '\n')` passes NO options object -> default flag 'a' (open/write/close, no fsync). A repo-wide grep for fsync|fdatasync|O_SYNC across src/ returns ZERO hits on the persistence path (only mcpServer.ts:64 audit-log `createWriteStream({flags:'a'})`, also unsynced, and baseWatcher.ts:82 a read-only `openSync(...,'r')`). memoryWrite (swarmMemory.ts:531) calls `persist(entry)` (574) -> appendShardLine (629/641) and returns the entry with no durability barrier. So on a true power loss / kernel panic within the OS page-cache flush window, acknowledged writes in the un-flushed tail are lost. That part of the finding is correct.

BUT THE BLAST RADIUS IS OVERSTATED — the finding's headline claim ("potentially the entire last burst written by the 90s/30-min ingest passes ... nothing re-drives those specific writes either") is FALSE for that exact vector, because the transcript corpus is self-healing on relaunch:
1) Watchers re-read from byte 0 every launch: claudeCodeWatcher.ts:260 / codexWatcher.ts:197 / geminiWatcher.ts:101 all call `tailFile(sessionFile, ...)` with NO `startAtEnd`, and offset is an in-memory `let offset = 0` (baseWatcher.ts:46) that is never persisted.
2) The 90s pass re-reads whole files, no persisted cursor: index.ts:1935 `fastIntervalMs: 90_000` -> `runConversationIngest({ hasHash: memoryHasHash, write: memoryWrite, ... })`; conversationIngest.ts:489 `readFile: (fp) => fsp.readFile(fp, 'utf8')` (entire file), dedup at :358 `if (deps.hasHash(chunk.hash))` using a stable sha256 key (:40 "sha256 over source+session+text — stable idempotent key").
3) Dedup reflects on-disk state only: swarmMemory.ts:376 `return ... (seenHashes.has(hash) || forgotSet.has(hash))`, and seenHashes is rebuilt purely from surviving disk lines in reloadFrom (swarmMemory.ts:199 per-line parse, :207 `if (e.hash && seenHashes.has(e.hash)) continue`, :210 `seenHashes.add(e.hash)`). So crash-tail chunks have hashes ABSENT after reload -> they are RE-WRITTEN within ~90s of next launch. The true source of truth (external Claude/Codex/Gemini transcript JSONL) is not written by Termpolis and survives the crash.

RESIDUAL GENUINE LOSS is small: only novel manual memory_write calls (decision/fact/result/note with no external file to re-scan) and control records — clear (swarmMemory.ts:1253), delete (:1313), reinforce (:1375) — written in the last flush window (seconds; up to ~30s Linux, ~1-5s typical Windows NTFS lazy writer), and ONLY on real power-loss/OS-crash, NOT on app crash or process.exit (page cache survives those; the finding correctly scoped its trigger). No corruption/cascade: entries are one independent JSON line each and reload parses per-line (swarmMemory.ts:199 `for (const line of raw.split('\n')) parseShardLine(...)`), so at worst the single torn tail line is dropped, never earlier entries.
verdict.notes: Verdict PARTIAL: the durability mechanism (no fsync — appendFileSync only) is correctly diagnosed and unrefutable, but the finding materially overstates impact and is wrong that "nothing re-drives those specific writes" — the very 90s/30-min transcript-ingest bursts it names are self-healing via re-tail-from-0 + whole-file re-read + seenHashes-rebuilt-from-disk dedup, sourced from external transcript files that survive the crash. Severity lowered medium->low: on a local Electron dev-tool RAG layer, worst realistic loss on a rare true power-loss is the last few seconds of NOVEL manual writes plus control deltas (a lost delete tombstone could resurrect a deleted memory; a lost reinforce delta is negligible). The proposed fix is still reasonable but should be scoped to control lines + novel high-value manual writes (decision/fact/result); fsync'ing the bulk kind:'message' ingest is largely wasted work given the recovery loop. Note the proposed fix's dependency on "finding #3 frame-repair" concerns torn-line cascade, which is a separate finding — for THIS finding, reload already isolates a torn tail line to itself (swarmMemory.ts:199).

title: 90-second active-session re-ingest deposits a new overlapping duplicate chunk on every turn (unstable trailing chunk)
failureScenario: The fast indexer re-ingests the ACTIVE session every 90s (index.ts:1935 fastIntervalMs=90_000, 1939 freshSinceTs=now-10min). chunkTurns is a single greedy forward pass that flushes a NOT-yet-full trailing buffer at the end (conversationIngest.ts:268 flush()), and makeChunk hashes the chunk TEXT (line 224 `${source}${sessionId}${text}`). Fully-packed chunks are stable across passes (earlier packing never depends on later turns), but the final partial chunk grows as new turns arrive: pass 1 stores partial B1=turns[7..9] (hash HB1); 90s later the user added turn 10, so re-chunking yields B2=turns[7..10] (hash HB2!=HB1) -> hasHash false -> WRITTEN, while B1 stays; next pass B3=turns[7..11]; etc. Each new turn in the fill cycle deposits one more strict-superset chunk while every prior partial lingers. Nothing prunes them: isForgettable requires kind==='message' AND age>=14 days (swarmMemory.ts:388-394), and these partials are brand-new (fresh ts).
whyItMatters: The most-recalled context — the live session — becomes the most polluted: memory_search returns a stack of overlapping near-identical copies of the same recent exchange, crowding out diverse hits, and (because ts is ingestion time) they all rank as freshest, compounding the known ts bug. Embeddings/RAM/disk are wasted linearly in turns.
proposedFix: Do not persist the trailing not-yet-full chunk on the incremental pass: emit only sealed (full) chunks and carry the tail forward to the next pass, or seal the final partial only when the session file is known complete (session ended). Alternatively delete superseded prefix chunks for a session when a superset chunk is written, or hash on stable turn-id boundaries so a growing tail reuses one identity.

verdict.evidence:
The trailing-partial re-ingest mechanism is REAL and reachable — no guard defeats it:

1) Fast tier fires every 90s on the active file. index.ts:1935-1939: `fastIntervalMs: 90_000,` ... `{ maxChunks: 250, freshSinceTs: Date.now() - 10 * 60_000 }`. memoryIndexer.ts:90: `fastInterval = setInterval(() => void scheduledTick(true), cfg.fastIntervalMs)`. The freshness filter INCLUDES the actively-written file (fresh mtime) — conversationIngest.ts:433-434: `if (freshSinceTs !== undefined) { try { if ((await fsp.stat(full)).mtimeMs < freshSinceTs) continue }`.

2) chunkTurns flushes the not-yet-full trailing buffer with no min-size guard. conversationIngest.ts:268 `flush()`; :246-249 `const flush = (): void => { if (buf.length === 0) return; const text = buf.map(...).join('\n\n').trim(); if (text) chunks.push(makeChunk(...)) }`. Seal condition depends only on already-seen turns (:264 `if (len > 0 && len + line.length + 2 > maxChars) flush()`), so sealed chunks are prefix-stable and only the tail grows.

3) makeChunk hashes the TEXT. conversationIngest.ts:222-224: `.update(`${source}${sessionId ?? ''}${text}`)`. A grown tail = new hash.

4) memoryWrite dedups by EXACT hash only; a grown tail misses and is embedded+persisted. swarmMemory.ts:546-550: `const effectiveHash = input.hash || contentHash(content); if (seenHashes.has(effectiveHash)) { const existing = entries.find(...); if (existing) return existing }`; :583 `if (stored.hash) seenHashes.add(stored.hash)`. No subset/superset detection.

5) Fresh copies are not reaped for 14 days. swarmMemory.ts:388-391: `minAgeMs = 14 * 86_400_000` ... `return entry.kind === 'message' && now - entry.ts >= minAgeMs && ...`.

NARROWER / LESS SEVERE than "high, every turn":
- A redundant chunk is deposited ONLY when a new turn EXTENDS an as-yet-unsealed <2000-char trailing window. When the next turn seals instead, flush() re-derives the identical prior partial (same turns/text) -> same hash -> correctly SKIPPED (swarmMemory.ts:547). Verbose turns each >~2000 chars self-seal/window (conversationIngest.ts:257-262) and create NO overlap. So it is the K-1 strict-prefix intermediate states of a window, not "every turn."
- Hot-window eviction of good memories is not a real harm: `const DEFAULT_MAX_ENTRIES = 500_000` (swarmMemory.ts:72), far above active-session duplicate counts. Durable cost is append-only disk/shard bloat (swarmMemory.ts:61-63 "append-only ... retains everything"), RAG search dilution, and wasted embeds.
- It is an AMPLIFIER, not a new bug: the pre-existing 30-min slow pass also re-reads the active file with no freshSinceTs and flushes the same trailing partial. index.ts:1904 `const stats = await runConversationIngest({ ... }, { maxChunks: 250 })` (no freshSinceTs). The 90s tier just makes it ~20x more frequent; the root cause is the chunker persisting an unsealed tail on every incremental pass.
verdict.notes: Reachable and unguarded, so NOT refuted. Downgraded high->medium because: (a) redundant writes occur only for turns extending an unsealed sub-2000-char window (sealing turns re-derive the identical prior partial and are skipped via seenHashes), not literally every turn; (b) 500k hot-window cap makes premature eviction of good memories a non-issue in practice; (c) real harm is append-only disk/shard bloat + RAG search dilution + wasted embeds during active sessions, and consolidation does tombstone the hot copies after 14 days. The proposed fix (emit only sealed chunks and carry the tail forward, or seal the final partial only when the session file is complete) is sound and correctly targets the chunker, which is the true root cause shared by BOTH the fast and slow passes.

title: Dedup check is not atomic across the embed await — two concurrent writes of identical content both insert a duplicate
failureScenario: memoryWrite checks seenHashes.has(effectiveHash) at line 547, then `await embed(content)` at line 570 (which yields the event loop), then finally entries.push + seenHashes.add at 582-583. Two concurrent writers of the SAME content interleave: both pass the line-547 check (neither has added the hash yet), both await embed, both then insert -> two entries with the same hash in the window and two lines on disk. Reachable in the product's core scenario: two swarm agents call MCP memory_write with the same fact in the same tick (index.ts:1092), or the user clicks 'Ingest conversations' (index.ts:1177) while the 90s fast pass (index.ts:1936) is mid-flight over the active session. The indexer's `running` guard (memoryIndexer.ts:49) only serializes the indexer's own passes — it does not cover these external memoryWrite entry points.
whyItMatters: Dedup exists specifically so a multi-agent swarm never stores the same fact twice, and it fails under exactly the concurrency the product is built around. The duplicate crowds search until the next reload; worse, if one copy is later deleted, memoryDelete removes the hash from seenHashes (line 1306) leaving the survivor permanently un-dedupable.
proposedFix: Reserve the hash synchronously before the await: on a line-547 miss, immediately add effectiveHash to seenHashes (or a dedicated in-flight set) so a concurrent writer sees it; re-check after embed and drop if another write already landed the hash. Or serialize memoryWrite through a single-consumer queue.

verdict.evidence:
The check-then-act across an await is real and reachable exactly as described.

MECHANISM (swarmMemory.ts):
- 547: `if (seenHashes.has(effectiveHash)) { const existing = entries.find(...) ; if (existing) return existing }`  (the check)
- 570: `const emb = await embed(content, false)`  (the sole yield; 531->570 and 574->583 are fully synchronous)
- 582-583: `entries.push(stored)` then `if (stored.hash) seenHashes.add(stored.hash)`  (reservation AFTER the await, with NO re-check of seenHashes post-embed)
Two writers both suspended at 570 both passed 547 and both unconditionally insert -> duplicate hash in the window + two JSONL lines.

THE AWAIT YIELDS (default config): embed() at 1529 executes `const emb = await embedText(text, { isQuery })` (1542) whenever `embeddingsAvailable !== false`, the documented normal state (1555-1557: "the bge model is bundled and normally loads"). Real async local-model inference spans a macrotask boundary -> wide window. (Only in the embedder-dead branch, 1540 `if (embeddingsAvailable === false) return null`, does it return before any await; that is not the default.)

NO SERIALIZATION AT ENTRY POINTS:
- MCP memory_write is served by a plain HTTP server (mcpServer.ts:649). Each request: `req.on('end', async () => { ... const response = await handleJsonRpc(request, handlers) ... })` (723, 741). `await handleJsonRpc` does not block a second concurrent request callback; only rate-LIMIT counters exist (704, 730), no mutex/queue. dispatch: 475-483 `case 'memory_write': return await handlers.memoryWrite({...})`.
- Manual ingest bypasses the indexer: index.ts:1179 `runConversationIngest({ hasHash: memoryHasHash, write: memoryWrite, ... })` is called DIRECTLY, not via tick(). The `running` guard (memoryIndexer.ts:49 `if (running) return { ... error: 'busy' }`) only wraps tick(), so it does not serialize manual ingest against the 90s fastRun (index.ts:1936) or IPC/MCP writes. The finding's guard-scope claim is correct.
- Ingest pre-check is itself non-atomic across passes: conversationIngest.ts:358 `if (deps.hasHash(chunk.hash)) { ...continue }` then 364 `await deps.write(chunk)` — two concurrent passes on the same chunk both miss and both write.

SEVERITY BOUND (finding did not note, keeps it at medium not higher): reloadFrom dedups by content hash on reload — swarmMemory.ts:207 `if (e.hash && seenHashes.has(e.hash)) continue`. So the in-window duplicate self-heals on next launch/sync-reload; persistent cost is a redundant on-disk line + a wasted embed + transient duplicate recall. Secondary effects that keep it a real medium: window-trim at 587 `if (dropped.hash) seenHashes.delete(dropped.hash)` can drop the hash while a surviving twin still holds it (defeating future dedup), and the discarded twin's auto-link edges (603-623) become dangling after reload.

Attempted refutations that FAILED: single-threaded JS does not help (await genuinely yields); no serializing lock/queue wraps memoryWrite at any entry point; embed yields in the default config; the `running` guard provably does not cover memory:write (IPC 1090), MCP memory_write (1769), or manual ingest (1179).
verdict.notes: Verdict CONFIRMED: the non-atomic dedup race is real and reachable through the product's core MCP path (two agents, same fact) and the unguarded manual-ingest-vs-scheduled-pass path. Every technical claim in the finding checks out, including that the indexer's `running` guard does not cover the external memoryWrite entry points. correctedSeverity kept at medium: the reloadFrom content-hash dedup (swarmMemory.ts:207) self-heals the in-window duplicate on next launch, so this is not permanent corruption — but a redundant on-disk line, a wasted embed, transient duplicate recall, plus the secondary seenHashes-delete-on-trim (587) and dangling auto-link edges keep it a legitimate medium rather than low. The proposed fix (synchronously reserve the hash in seenHashes/an in-flight set on the 547 miss before awaiting, then re-check/drop after embed) is the correct shape.

title: contentHash collapses all whitespace, so whitespace-significant content (e.g. Python) false-dedups and the second write is silently lost
failureScenario: contentHash normalizes with `.replace(/\s+/g, ' ').trim()` (line 527), collapsing every run of spaces/tabs/newlines to one space. An agent stores snippet A via memory_write: `def f():\n    return risky()` then snippet B `def f():\n        return risky()` (deeper indentation -> different nesting/behavior). Both normalize to `def f(): return risky()` -> identical hash -> B hits seenHashes and returns A (line 549); B is never stored. Same for YAML, diffs, Markdown code fences, or ASCII tables where whitespace is semantic.
whyItMatters: Memory silently loses genuinely distinct content and hands back the wrong version — the 'never silently lie' guarantee is broken for any content where whitespace carries meaning, which for a developer tool is common.
proposedFix: Do not collapse newlines/indentation in the identity hash. Normalize only Unicode form plus trailing whitespace (e.g. NFC + per-line right-trim), or hash the raw content. Keep whitespace-collapse as a separate near-duplicate SIGNAL, never as the identity key.

verdict.evidence:
The MECHANISM is real and reachable, but the finding overstates severity and its flagship example is invalid.

REAL & REACHABLE (not refuted):
- swarmMemory.ts:527 `const normalized = (content || '').normalize('NFC').replace(/\s+/g, ' ').trim()` — collapses every run of spaces/tabs/newlines to one space, so whitespace-only-different content maps to one hash.
- swarmMemory.ts:546 `const effectiveHash = input.hash || contentHash(content)` — direct writes without a supplied hash use this collapsing hash as the dedup key.
- swarmMemory.ts:547-549 `if (seenHashes.has(effectiveHash)) { const existing = entries.find(e => e.hash === effectiveHash); if (existing) return existing }` — on a hit it returns the FIRST entry and skips embed/persist/index; no dedup flag is returned, so the second distinct content is silently dropped.
- Agent-facing path confirmed to omit hash: mcpServer.ts:476-483 (memory_write MCP tool forwards agentId/kind/content/tags/taskId/project only) and index.ts:1769-1785 (handler forwards the same, no hash) -> contentHash is genuinely used for direct agent writes. Unguarded.

WHY PARTIAL / LESS SEVERE THAN CLAIMED (medium -> low):
1. The finding's own example is factually wrong. A `def f():\n    return risky()` (4 spaces) vs B `def f():\n        return risky()` (8 spaces) are SEMANTICALLY IDENTICAL Python — indent width of a single-statement body is irrelevant; there is no "different nesting/behavior." The example demonstrates dedup of two identical programs (arguably the desired behavior), not loss of distinct content. A VALID example would be block membership: `if x:\n a()\n b()` vs `if x:\n a()\nb()`, which both collapse to `if x: a() b()` yet differ in behavior.
2. The collapse is DELIBERATE and documented: swarmMemory.ts:521-525 "We normalize Unicode form and collapse/trim whitespace so trivially different copies (reflowed, padded) of the same text map to one entry." Default write kind is prose ('note'), where collapse is benign/intended.
3. Ingested code/transcripts are NOT affected: codeIngest.ts:79-83 hashes the RAW body (`update('code'+filePath+startLine+body)`) and passes it as input.hash at codeIngest.ts:184; conversationIngest.ts:222-224 hashes raw text and passes it at conversationIngest.ts:498. Both bypass contentHash. So the bulk of code/transcript content in memory is immune; only hand-authored direct memory_write calls are in scope.
4. Real data loss therefore needs the narrow intersection: two direct writes differing ONLY in whitespace AND where that whitespace is load-bearing (Python block membership, YAML nesting, ASCII tables). Real, but uncommon, and silent when it happens.

Net: the identity hash genuinely cannot distinguish semantically-significant whitespace, so the proposed fix (per-line right-trim + NFC as identity, whitespace-collapse only as a near-dup SIGNAL) is a legitimate improvement — but the impact is a narrow, low-severity edge case, not the broad medium-severity loss the example implies.
verdict.notes: Cannot REFUTE: contentHash's whitespace collapse (line 527) is the real dedup key for direct agent writes (line 546), and a collision returns the first entry and drops the second (lines 547-549), reachable via the default memory_write MCP tool with no hash override (mcpServer.ts:476-483, index.ts:1769-1785). Downgraded to low because: the finding's Python example is semantically identical (no behavior difference, so not a valid data-loss demo); the collapse is an intentional documented design choice for merging reflowed/padded copies (lines 521-525); ingestion paths carry raw-content hashes and are unaffected (codeIngest.ts:184, conversationIngest.ts:498); and genuine loss needs the narrow case of two writes differing only in load-bearing whitespace. Note it IS silent (no error, stale entry returned), which keeps it above 'none'.

title: Worker embed that resolves null (crash/exit/model-absent-in-worker) is treated as SUCCESS, so the in-process fallback is skipped and semantic memory silently dies
failureScenario: Production wires a real worker_thread (index.ts:1672 `setWorkerSpawner(() => createWorkerTransport())`, spawned lazily on first embed). The worker embeds one text per message; on the main side, `createWorkerTransport` (embedWorker.ts:43-45) installs `failAll = () => { for (const resolve of pending.values()) resolve(null) }` on BOTH the worker 'error' and 'exit' events — i.e. a worker crash RESOLVES the pending embed with `null`, it does not reject. Step by step: (1) The embedding worker crashes mid-request — e.g. an onnxruntime-web WASM fault/OOM during `session.run` on a pathological chunk, or the worker's own model load returns null so its `embedText` yields null (embedWorker.ts:22). (2) `w.embed(text)` resolves to `null`. (3) In `tryWorkerEmbed` the `Promise.race` resolves (no throw), so it returns `{ ok: true, vec: null }` (line 282) — a null vector is reported as a SUCCESSFUL embed. (4) In `embedBatch` the worker loop (lines 349-354) sees `r.ok === true`, pushes `null`, keeps `ok = true`, and returns `[null]` WITHOUT ever reaching the in-process `getBackend()` fallback below. (5) `embedText` returns null; `swarmMemory.embed()` treats null as a dead embedder and latches `embeddingsAvailable = false` (swarmMemory.ts:1544). Result: a single worker crash converts the entire session to keyword-only recall, and the perfectly-good in-process backend is never tried — the exact opposite of the design contract quoted at localEmbedder.ts:239-240 and index.ts:1669-1671 ("any spawn/timeout/failure disables the worker and falls back to the in-process embedder").
whyItMatters: The worker layer was added purely as a main-thread-offload optimization and was explicitly promised to be recall-safe ("recall cannot regress"). Because a null-resolving worker is indistinguishable from success here, a transient worker fault silently downgrades the product's core value (semantic memory) to keyword search for the whole session — and unlike the timeout path (which correctly returns ok:false and falls back), this path never even consults the working in-process embedder. The tests only cover the worker THROWING (localEmbedder.test.ts:327), never the worker resolving null, so this gap is unguarded.
proposedFix: Treat a null worker result as a miss, not a success. In `tryWorkerEmbed` return `{ ok: vec !== null, vec }` (localEmbedder.ts:282) so `embedBatch` breaks and falls through to the in-process backend; and/or in `embedWorker.ts` change `failAll` to REJECT pending promises on 'error'/'exit' (lines 43-45) so a crash surfaces as a real failure. Add a unit test where the injected worker resolves null and assert the in-process backend is used.

verdict.evidence:
Every link in the chain verified against real code; the primary scenario is reachable and defeats the stated "recall cannot regress" contract.

(1) localEmbedder.ts:282 — inside tryWorkerEmbed: `return { ok: true, vec }`. Returns ok:true even when vec is null; there is no `vec !== null` check anywhere (grep confirms line 282 is the only `ok: true` on the worker path).

(2) localEmbedder.ts:349-355 — worker loop: `for (const p of prepared) { const r = await tryWorkerEmbed(p); if (!r.ok) { ok = false; break }; out.push(r.vec) } if (ok) { noteWorkerStatus(true); return out }`. A {ok:true, vec:null} pushes null, keeps ok=true, and returns [null] WITHOUT reaching the in-process `getBackend()` fallback at line 357-358.

(3) embedWorker.ts:43-45 — `const failAll = (): void => { for (const resolve of pending.values()) resolve(null); pending.clear() }` bound to BOTH `worker.on('error', failAll)` and `worker.on('exit', failAll)`. A worker crash RESOLVES the in-flight embed with null (does not reject). Line 22 `try { vec = await embedText(...) } catch { vec = null }` + line 41 `resolve(m.vec)` means a worker model-load null likewise arrives as a resolved null.

(4) swarmMemory.ts:1540-1552 — `if (embeddingsAvailable === false) return null` ... `const emb = await embedText(text,{isQuery}); if (!emb || emb.length > MAX_EMBEDDING_DIM) { embeddingsAvailable = false; return null }`. A single null latches embeddingsAvailable=false, and line 1540 then short-circuits ALL future embeds for the session.

(5) swarmMemory.ts:249 & 308 — the ONLY resets of embeddingsAvailable to null are inside initSwarmMemory and _resetForTests. There is no periodic re-probe, so the latch is permanent for the running session. Confirms "single worker crash converts the entire session to keyword-only."

(6) index.ts:1672 — `try { setWorkerSpawner(() => createWorkerTransport()) } catch {...}` wires the real worker in production (lazy on first embed). index.ts:1669-1671 and localEmbedder.ts:239-240 explicitly promise the fallback ("any spawn/timeout/failure disables the worker and falls back to in-process ... recall cannot regress") — which the null-as-success bug violates.

Reachability: the primary trigger (onnxruntime-web WASM fault/OOM during session.run, most likely on the FIRST embed's cold model load in the worker) resolves the pending embed to null via failAll; the main-side in-process backend that would have loaded fine from process.resourcesPath is bypassed, and swarmMemory silently latches the session to keyword-only. Reachable and net-harmful.

Nuance (does not refute): the sub-trigger "worker's own model load returns null" only adds harm if the worker_thread resolves the model differently than the main process (process.resourcesPath/cwd differing in the worker); if identical, worker-fails implies main-also-fails so the skipped fallback wouldn't have helped. The crash-after-successful-load path carries no such caveat, so the finding stands. The proposed fix (`return { ok: vec !== null, vec }` at localEmbedder.ts:282, and/or REJECT in embedWorker.ts failAll) is correct and currently absent.
verdict.notes: Severity high (not critical): no data loss/corruption or crash — it is a silent, session-persistent degradation of a core feature (semantic recall) that specifically defeats the explicit "recall cannot regress" safety contract, and is most likely to fire on the memory-constrained machines the worker was added to help (cold-load OOM on first embed). Likelihood is failure-gated (needs a worker null), so a strictly likelihood-weighted reviewer could argue medium, but the large per-occurrence blast radius plus the silent, unrecoverable-within-session nature justifies high. Fully unguarded: no existing test or code path treats a null worker result as a miss.

title: embeddingsAvailable latches false permanently on the FIRST null/failed embed — one transient inference error disables the semantic brain for the whole session with no retry
failureScenario: `embed()` caches a single boolean and never re-probes: line 1540 `if (embeddingsAvailable === false) return null` short-circuits every future call, and both the null-result branch (1543-1546) and the catch branch (1549-1551) set `embeddingsAvailable = false`. Grep confirms it is only ever reset to null at initSwarmMemory/reset (lines 249, 308) — there is NO periodic re-probe. Concrete trigger without any worker: (1) The in-process backend throws ONCE — `be(bucket)` raising a transient onnxruntime-web WASM runtime error under momentary memory pressure, or `loadDefaultBackend` throwing once on first load because the .onnx file is briefly locked by Windows Defender's on-access scan. (2) That single throw makes `embedText` return null for that call (embedBatch leaves the slot null / getBackend returns null). Note this ALSO trips a second permanent latch inside localEmbedder: a load throw calls `markFailed()` → `loadFailed = true` (localEmbedder.ts:115-119, 224), after which `getBackend()` returns null forever (line 110). (3) `swarmMemory.embed()` sets `embeddingsAvailable = false`. (4) From then on, for the remainder of the session, EVERY memoryWrite stores an entry with no embedding and EVERY memorySearch runs keyword-only — even though the model would now load and run fine. Only an app relaunch (re-init) clears it, and if the root cause is deterministic the relaunch reproduces it.
whyItMatters: A memory brain that must 'never silently lie' instead flips itself into permanent keyword-only mode on the first hiccup and, because the flag is sticky, denies itself any recovery. Every fact written during the degraded window is persisted vector-less to disk (see the companion backfill finding), so the damage outlives the transient error and even outlives the session. This is the same CLASS as the confirmed ts bug: a silent, sticky degradation of stored-memory quality that misleads every later recall.
proposedFix: Do not cache `false` as a terminal state from a single per-call null. Either re-probe each call (localEmbedder already owns the truly-dead latch via `loadFailed`, so swarmMemory caching false is redundant and harmful), or replace the boolean with a bounded retry/backoff that periodically re-attempts, or only latch false when `isEmbedderReady()===false AND a load was actually attempted`. Also call `recordSwarmError('swarmMemory.embed.failed', ...)` on the transition so the degradation is observable.

verdict.evidence:
The latch is real, structurally proven, and the trigger is reachable with the underlying embedder staying healthy.

STRUCTURAL LATCH (src/main/swarmMemory.ts):
- L88: `let embeddingsAvailable: boolean | null = null  // cached probe result`
- L1540: `if (embeddingsAvailable === false) return null  // forced off / known-dead` — this short-circuits BEFORE the L1542 `embedText` call, so the recovery write at L1547 `embeddingsAvailable = true` is UNREACHABLE once false. One-way latch.
- Null branch L1543-1546: `if (!emb || emb.length > MAX_EMBEDDING_DIM) { embeddingsAvailable = false; return null }`
- Catch branch L1549-1551: `} catch { embeddingsAvailable = false; return null }`
- Grep for `embeddingsAvailable` shows the ONLY writes back to null are L249 (`initSwarmMemory`) and L308 (a full teardown reset at L285-313 that also nulls `userDataDir`/`deviceId` — effectively test/teardown). No periodic re-probe. Production auto-reset is `initSwarmMemory` only, called at app startup (index.ts:1884) and in `setSyncDir` (swarmMemory.ts:1518, a manual user action). Finding's "only app relaunch clears it" is accurate.

CALLERS DEGRADE AS DESCRIBED:
- memoryWrite L570-571: `const emb = await embed(content, false); if (emb) entry.embedding = emb` — after the latch, entries persist with NO embedding. Note this is PERMANENT data damage: entries written during the outage stay embedding-less even after a relaunch until re-ingested.
- memorySearch L887-890: `try { queryEmb = await embed(opts.query, true) } catch {}` then `if (queryEmb) {...vector...}` — null queryEmb skips the vector block → keyword-only.

TRIGGER REACHABLE, BACKEND STAYS HEALTHY (src/main/localEmbedder.ts):
- embedBatch L360-368: `for (const bucket ...) { try { const vecs = await be(...) ... } catch { /* leave this bucket's slots null */ } }`. A transient runtime throw from `be(bucket)` (e.g. onnxruntime-web WASM OOM under memory pressure) is swallowed here; the slot stays null but `backend` (L65/L218) and `loadFailed` (L67) are NOT touched, and `markFailed()` (L115-119) is NOT called. So embedText returns null ONCE while the loaded backend remains fully usable — getBackend() (L104-113) would return the same live `backend` on the next call. swarmMemory then latches false forever: the latch is the SOLE cause of non-recovery, exactly matching the finding's "even though the model would now load and run fine."

ADVERSARIAL CHECKS THAT DID NOT SAVE THE CODE:
- The most mundane trigger (empty text → embedText L230 `if (!text || !text.trim()) return null`) is CLOSED upstream: memoryWrite L532 throws on empty content, memorySearch L863 returns [] on empty query. So the trigger genuinely requires a real backend fault — but that fault path is intact and unguarded against re-probe.
- Load-throw trigger (loadDefaultBackend L199 `InferenceSession.create` throwing on a Defender-locked .onnx → markFailed → loadFailed=true) also reaches the latch; here localEmbedder is independently dead too (the finding concedes this), so it is internally consistent.
- OBSERVABILITY GAP CONFIRMED: `recordSwarmError` is imported (swarmMemory.ts:4) and used at L277 (init.failed) and L636 (persist.failed) but is NOT called in `embed()`. The only signal of the degradation is a passive SLI at index.ts:1121 `recordMetric({ t: 'embed', available: embeddingsReady() })`, recorded only on UI recalls — no error event on the false-transition, supporting the finding's fix.

Minor imprecisions in the finding that do not affect reachability or severity: it labels L308 as "reset" (it is a full teardown, not a live re-probe) and omits the incidental setSyncDir re-init path; it implies zero observability though a passive embed SLI exists. None of these provide auto-recovery.

SEVERITY: high. This is a fault-triggered resilience defect (does not fire on a clean run — normal load flips it true and it stays true), so likelihood is bounded by how often the backend transiently throws/nulls. But when it fires the blast radius is severe and sticky: entire session forced keyword-only, entries written during the window permanently lose embeddings, no user-visible error, and NO retry — and the plausible triggers (WASM OOM under load with many terminals; Defender on-access lock of a freshly-written model on Windows, a concern the code comments at localEmbedder.ts:11-13 explicitly call out) are exactly the field conditions that never reproduce in CI. High is the appropriate call; a reviewer could defensibly place it at the high end of medium given the fault precondition.
verdict.notes: Verified against real code at C:/Users/DavidEngelhart/repos/termpolis. Finding is accurate. Fix direction is sound: for the runtime-throw case swarmMemory's cached false is both redundant-with-nothing (localEmbedder is still healthy) and harmful — dropping the swarmMemory cache and deferring to localEmbedder's own loadFailed latch (or a bounded retry/backoff) would restore auto-recovery, and adding recordSwarmError on the transition closes the observability gap.

title: Entries written while the embedder is down are never back-filled, and content-hash dedup blocks any refresh — they stay permanently excluded from semantic (vector) recall
failureScenario: There is no re-embed/backfill pass anywhere (verified by grep across src/main). Once the embedder has been down (dev without the model, a broken install, or after either latch finding above), the store permanently contains vector-less entries that never recover: (1) During a down-window, `memoryWrite` computes `embed()` → null (best-effort, swarmMemory.ts:568-572), so the entry is persisted to disk and pushed to the hot window with NO embedding and is never added to the packed vectorStore. (2) The embedder later recovers (relaunch, model finishes downloading, transient error clears). (3) The same content is written again — extremely common: agents re-state facts, and the auto-indexer re-ingests overlapping transcripts every launch. `memoryWrite`'s dedup returns the EXISTING vector-less entry before the embed block (lines 547-550: `if (seenHashes.has(effectiveHash)) { ... return existing }`), so it is never embedded. (4) In `memorySearch`, with a healthy 384-dim query, the packed path scores only embedded entries; the legacy loop skips entries with no `.embedding` (line 932); and the keyword safety-net only runs `if (scored.length === 0)` (line 937), which is false whenever any embedded entry matched. So the vector-less entries can surface ONLY via the BM25 lexical fusion (exact-token overlap, line 949+) — never via semantic similarity. A paraphrased query can never retrieve them.
whyItMatters: The store silently and permanently splits into first-class (semantically recallable) and second-class (keyword-only) memories with no reconciliation. A fact captured during a model outage is invisible to exactly the paraphrase/semantic queries that RAG exists to serve, and dedup guarantees it can never be upgraded. This is a durable, on-disk, cross-session degradation of stored-memory quality — the same solidity class as the confirmed ts bug.
proposedFix: Add an idempotent backfill: on the dedup hit, if the existing entry lacks a packed vector and the embedder is now available, compute and index its embedding before returning (swarmMemory.ts:547-550). Additionally, run a bounded background pass on launch that embeds any hot-window entry lacking a vector once `isEmbedderReady()` is true.

verdict.evidence:
Every link in the chain is present in real code, and all cited line numbers are accurate.

1) Dedup returns the existing entry BEFORE any embed attempt. swarmMemory.ts:546-550:
```
const effectiveHash = input.hash || contentHash(content)
if (seenHashes.has(effectiveHash)) {
  const existing = entries.find(e => e.hash === effectiveHash)
```
