```
  if (existing) return existing
}
```
The embed block sits AFTER this at 568-572, so a re-write of already-seen content never embeds.

2) Down-window writes persist vector-less. swarmMemory.ts:568-572 `try { const emb = await embed(content,false); if (emb) entry.embedding = emb } catch {}` — null embed leaves `entry.embedding` unset. indexEntryVector then early-returns (line 649: `if (!entry.embedding || entry.embedding.length !== EMBED_DIM) return`), so nothing is added to vectorStore. The entry is still persisted (574) and pushed to the hot window (582).

3) The embedder latches OFF for the whole process — a strong amplifier. swarmMemory.ts:1540 `if (embeddingsAvailable === false) return null`, set at 1544/1550 on the first null/throw. One transient embed failure makes every subsequent write that session permanently vector-less until relaunch.

4) No re-embed on reload. initSwarmMemory→reloadFrom (188) pushes entries as-read then calls rebuildVectorIndex() (216); rebuildVectorIndex (660-667) only does `for (const e of entries){ indexEntryVector(e); lexicalIndex.add(...) }` — indexEntryVector packs an EXISTING vector or early-returns; it never computes one. So a vector-less entry survives every relaunch vector-less.

5) Search can only reach these via BM25, never semantics. Packed path (894-928) scans vectorStore only (entry absent). Legacy loop 931-934: `if (!entry.embedding || entry.embedding.length !== queryEmb.length) continue`. Keyword safety net gated at 937 `if (scored.length === 0)` — false whenever any embedded entry matched. Vector-less entries ARE in the lexical index (added on write at 581 and on reload at 665), so the only path that surfaces them is the BM25 fusion at 949-972 (exact-token overlap). A paraphrased query with no shared tokens can never retrieve them.

6) No embedding backfill exists anywhere. Grep over src for `!e.embedding`/reembed/backfill-embed yields only the three SKIP sites (649, 932, 1207) — none embed. The only hash-keyed backfill is memoryPatchProjects (396-415), which patches `project` slugs, never vectors. The auto-indexer (memoryIndexer.ts) is pure scheduling over a content-hash-deduped ingest ("repeated runs only embed genuinely new chunks"), and ingest also skips already-stored hashes at the ingest layer (IngestDeps.hasHash), so re-ingesting a transcript first captured during a down-window is doubly locked out of re-embedding.

Nuance (does not change the verdict): the auto-ingest trigger is the reliable one — source-scoped hashes are deterministic, so re-ingest hits dedup verbatim every launch. The "agents re-state facts" trigger is weaker: contentHash (526-528) preserves wording, so a genuinely paraphrased restatement produces a NEW hash and DOES get embedded when healthy; only verbatim restatement stays vector-less. Affected entries also remain keyword/exact-token recoverable, so this is permanent loss of SEMANTIC recall, not total loss.
verdict.notes: Verdict CONFIRMED, severity medium upheld. Blast radius is bounded to down-windows (dev without the bundled model, broken install, or the embeddingsAvailable latch flipping false on a transient error) — a healthy install flips embeddingsAvailable=true on the first write and never hits this. What justifies medium over low: (a) permanence — no pass ever backfills, so affected entries are semantic-dead across all future launches; (b) the process-wide latch at swarmMemory.ts:1540 means a single transient embed failure poisons an entire session's writes, a realistic production trigger; (c) the system's own idempotency (ingest hasHash skip + memoryWrite dedup at 547-550) actively prevents recovery. Not higher because entries remain fully recoverable via BM25 exact-token search. The proposed fix (backfill the vector on a dedup hit when the embedder is ready, plus a bounded launch pass over hot-window entries lacking a packed vector) is sound and idempotent; it would also want to cover the ingest-layer hasHash short-circuit so re-ingest actually reaches the backfill.

title: No dimension contract between the embedder output and EMBED_DIM (MAX_EMBEDDING_DIM=1024 ≠ EMBED_DIM=384) — a model/dim change silently drops vectors to the slow path or makes the packed store unsearchable
failureScenario: The embed accept-gate and the index/search gates use DIFFERENT dimensions and there is no assertion that the model actually outputs EMBED_DIM. `embed()` accepts any vector with `length <= MAX_EMBEDDING_DIM` (1024) (swarmMemory.ts:1534, 1543), but `indexEntryVector` only packs vectors with `length === EMBED_DIM` (384) and silently drops everything else to the per-object 'legacy' path (line 649: `if (... entry.embedding.length !== EMBED_DIM) return`), and both search fast-paths are gated on `queryEmb.length === EMBED_DIM` (lines 894, 1190). Meanwhile `loadDefaultBackend` trusts whatever hidden size the ONNX file reports — `const H = hidden.dims[hidden.dims.length - 1]` (localEmbedder.ts:215-216) with no check against EMBED_DIM. Scenario: a release accidentally bundles bge-BASE (768-dim) instead of bge-small, or a future version bumps the model. (1) `embed()` now returns 768-dim vectors (768 <= 1024, so accepted; embeddingsAvailable=true — looks healthy). (2) New writes fail the `=== 384` check, so nothing is ever added to the packed vectorStore and the number[] is never freed (RAM regression). (3) Queries are 768-dim, so `queryEmb.length === EMBED_DIM` is false and the entire packed fast-path is skipped; any pre-existing 384-dim packed vectors become unreachable (query dim never matches). No error is raised at any step. Recall silently collapses onto the legacy per-object scan / BM25.
whyItMatters: The packed vector store is the primary semantic index, and its correctness silently depends on an un-asserted equality between a hardcoded constant and the model's real output dimension. A wrong bundled model or a dim change produces no error, no telemetry, and a quietly broken index — the classic 'dim mismatch' robustness failure, made worse because the two dimension constants openly disagree so the mismatch is not even caught at the accept-gate.
proposedFix: Assert the contract: in `loadDefaultBackend`, verify the first forward pass yields H === EMBED_DIM and treat a mismatch as a hard load failure (markFailed + telemetry); set MAX_EMBEDDING_DIM = EMBED_DIM (or make embed() reject `length !== EMBED_DIM`) so a non-conforming vector can never be accepted; and stamp the store/HNSW fingerprint with the model dim so a dimension change invalidates the index instead of silently mixing dims.

verdict.evidence:
All code citations in the finding are ACCURATE: localEmbedder.ts:26 `export const EMBED_DIM = 384`; swarmMemory.ts:75 `const MAX_EMBEDDING_DIM = 1024`; embed() accept-gate swarmMemory.ts:1534 `if (r.length > MAX_EMBEDDING_DIM) return null` and :1543 `if (!emb || emb.length > MAX_EMBEDDING_DIM) {`; pack-gate swarmMemory.ts:649 `if (!entry.embedding || entry.embedding.length !== EMBED_DIM) return`; search fast-path gates swarmMemory.ts:894 and :1190 `if (queryEmb.length === EMBED_DIM && vectorStore.size > 0)`; and localEmbedder.ts:215-216 `const H = hidden.dims[hidden.dims.length - 1]` / `return meanPoolNormalize(..., H)` with no EMBED_DIM assertion (also none in meanPoolNormalize:156-183 or embedText:229-233). So the underlying observation — no dimension contract asserting the model outputs EMBED_DIM — is REAL and correctly located, not a misread.

But the finding is narrower/less severe than claimed on two counts:

(1) NOT REACHABLE under shipped defaults. The model is hardcoded: localEmbedder.ts:32-33 `const MODEL_DIR_NAME = 'bge-small-en-v1.5'` / `const ONNX_MODEL_FILE = 'model_quantized.onnx'`. resolveAssetDir (124-143) only *locates* that bundled 384-dim model in fixed paths (resourcesPath/models, cwd/resources/models, transformers cache) — there is no env/config/user seam to swap in a different-dim model. So H === 384 in every shipped build and NONE of the failure chain fires. The scenario is entirely contingent on the auditor's own hypothetical ("a release accidentally bundles bge-BASE … or a future version bumps the model"), i.e. a future code change / mis-bundle, not current input, data, or config.

(2) Impact OVERSTATED. The claim "Recall silently collapses onto the legacy per-object scan / BM25" is wrong for the primary (uniform-swap) case. The legacy paths gate on query dim, NOT EMBED_DIM: swarmMemory.ts:932 `if (!entry.embedding || entry.embedding.length !== queryEmb.length) continue` → `cosineSimilarity(queryEmb, entry.embedding)`, and swarmMemory.ts:1207 same in nearestNeighbours. So if a swapped model produced uniform 768-dim vectors, new writes stay as number[] on the entry and a 768-dim query matches them → semantic cosine search KEEPS WORKING (degraded only in speed/RAM: O(n), no HNSW, number[] not freed). Only a MIXED-dim store (swap mid-life) makes pre-existing packed 384-dim vectors semantically unreachable — and even those remain lexically recallable because rebuildVectorIndex indexes every entry's content into the always-on lexical index (swarmMemory.ts:665 `for (const e of entries) { indexEntryVector(e); lexicalIndex.add(e.id, e.content) }`). So the true worst case is: loss of SEMANTIC (not lexical) recall for OLD packed vectors, only in a mixed-dim store, only after a hypothetical model change.

Net: a legitimate but latent defense-in-depth gap (a cheap H===EMBED_DIM load assertion + store dim fingerprint would be sound), not an active or reachable bug in the shipped product; self-rated severity low is correct.
verdict.notes: Verified callers/definitions across swarmMemory.ts (embed accept-gate, indexEntryVector, both search paths, rebuildVectorIndex) and localEmbedder.ts (loadDefaultBackend, meanPoolNormalize, resolveAssetDir/resolveOnnxModel, model constants). No test asserts model output dim against EMBED_DIM (grep for 384/hidden.dims in *.test.ts: no matches), so a future swap would indeed be uncaught by CI — but the model is not swappable via any shipped config, so the scenario cannot trigger today. Verdict PARTIAL rather than CONFIRMED (not an active/reachable bug) and not REFUTED (the no-dimension-contract observation is factually correct and the proposed load-time assertion is a valid hardening).

title: Unbounded `clearedBefore` epoch = one bad clock (or one corrupt line) permanently wipes the whole brain on every device and silently locks out all future writes
failureScenario: 1) A user's machine has a wrong clock (dead CMOS battery / manual misconfig / VM with drifted RTC) reading year 2099, or a shard line is corrupted/hand-edited so `clearedBefore` is huge. 2) On that machine `memoryClear()` runs (`memory:clear` IPC, index.ts:1140), executing `clearEpoch = Date.now()` (line 1252) and appending `{"clearedBefore": 4102444800000}` to the shard (line 1253). 3) That shard syncs everywhere. 4) On EVERY device, `parseShardLine` does `if (obj.clearedBefore > clearEpoch) clearEpoch = obj.clearedBefore` with NO upper bound (line 172), so clearEpoch jumps to the year-2099 value. 5) `reloadFrom` then drops every entry via `if ((e.ts || 0) <= clearEpoch) continue` (line 206) — all real memories (ts ~1.7e12 < 4.1e12) vanish. 6) The poison line is append-only and persists forever, and `reloadFrom` resets clearEpoch to 0 then re-derives it from that line on EVERY reload (30-min timer, index.ts:1903), so the wipe re-applies indefinitely. 7) Worse, every NEW write also gets `ts: Date.now()` ~1.7e12 (line 554) which is still <= clearEpoch, so it is swallowed on the next reload — the brain permanently refuses to remember anything new. Reinforcement deltas are discarded too (`r.ts <= clearEpoch`, line 223).
whyItMatters: A single device with a mis-set clock, or a single corrupted/edited shard byte, silently and permanently destroys the entire shared memory on all devices AND disables all future learning, with no UI path to recover (only manual shard-file surgery). This is the maximal 'memory silently loses all data' failure and it is reachable via an ordinary clock misconfiguration, not just deliberate corruption.
proposedFix: Never trust an unbounded wall-clock epoch. On merge, clamp/reject absurd values: `if (obj.clearedBefore > clearEpoch && obj.clearedBefore <= Date.now() + MAX_SKEW) clearEpoch = obj.clearedBefore`. Better, stop using a wall-clock cutoff for clears entirely: have `memoryClear` enumerate the concrete set of currently-live entry ids into tombstones, or issue a monotonic per-device logical clear COUNTER tagged with the issuing deviceId, so a mis-clocked machine cannot poison the global epoch. Also persist a device-local monotonic floor so a bogus future epoch can be detected and refused.

verdict.evidence:
Every cited line verified in real code; there is NO upper bound / clock-skew clamp anywhere on the clearedBefore merge or on entry ts.

1) Unbounded merge (the defect) — swarmMemory.ts:172:
   `if (typeof obj.clearedBefore === 'number') { if (obj.clearedBefore > clearEpoch) clearEpoch = obj.clearedBefore; return }`
   Only a monotonic MAX; no ceiling, no `Date.now()+MAX_SKEW` guard, no sanity cap.

2) Wipe on reload — swarmMemory.ts:206:
   `if ((e.ts || 0) <= clearEpoch) continue         // cleared epoch`
   Real entries (ts ~1.7e12) < a year-2099 poison (4.1e12) ⇒ all dropped.

3) memoryClear writes an unbounded wall-clock epoch, in sync mode — swarmMemory.ts:1249-1253:
   `if (syncDir) { ... clearEpoch = Date.now(); appendShardLine(JSON.stringify({ clearedBefore: clearEpoch }), 'clear') }`
   Local-only mode instead truncates (1255), so the poison-line path is the sync branch (or a hand-edited line).

4) Re-applied every reload, persists forever — swarmMemory.ts:192 resets `clearEpoch = 0` then 172 re-derives it from the append-only line every time; reloadMemoryFromSync (1392-1394: `if (!syncDir) return; reloadFrom(shardFiles())`) is driven by the 30-min indexer (index.ts:1903 `reloadMemoryFromSync()`). Shards are append-only (appendShardLine, 629-638) so the line is never removed.

5) New writes silently swallowed — swarmMemory.ts:554 `ts: input.ts ?? Date.now()` (no upper clamp) ⇒ every new entry ts <= poison epoch ⇒ dropped on next reloadFrom. Reinforcement deltas too — 223: `if (tombstones.has(r.id) || r.ts <= clearEpoch || !liveIds.has(r.id)) continue`.

6) Reachability is real, not dead code: memory:clear IPC (index.ts:1140); sync is a shipped user feature — memory:set-sync-dir + native folder picker (index.ts:1294-1308, dialog literally says "e.g. inside Dropbox or Syncthing"), preload memorySetSyncDir (preload/index.ts:153), Memory.tsx UI (62).

7) The threat model is KNOWN yet not applied here: memoryEconomy.ts:111 "`deltaT` is clamped >= 0 so a future-dated synced-peer clock can't manufacture a boost" and mnemeConsolidate.ts:65 same — the authors deliberately clamp future-dated peer clocks in the ranking math, but applied NO analogous guard to the clearedBefore epoch merge (172). Grep for MAX_SKEW/clock/skew finds guards only in ranking, never on the clear epoch or on ts.
verdict.notes:
Confirmed real and reachable; the fix (clamp `clearedBefore <= Date.now()+MAX_SKEW`) is trivial and one the authors already use elsewhere. Honest calibration of preconditions (narrower than the one-line title, but the finding's detailed body already states them, so this is not a misread):

- The amplified "wipes every device, silent 30-min re-apply" version requires OPT-IN sync mode (default is local-only, swarmMemory.ts:82). This lowers likelihood vs a default-on feature — the main reason a reviewer might argue "high." I keep critical because impact is maximal/global/irreversible and the corrupt-line vector is realistic.
- Clock path also needs memoryClear() to actually run on the mis-clocked machine (a bad clock alone writes nothing). It is user-initiated via the "clear" button.
- The "dead CMOS battery" example is directionally weak: CMOS usually resets to a PAST date (BIOS build date), which writes a clearedBefore in the PAST (< real entries' ts) = harmless. The dangerous trigger is a FUTURE clock (VM RTC drift forward, manual misconfig, NTP glitch) OR — most realistically — a corrupt/hand-edited shard line (clock- and clear-independent), plausible because shards are plaintext JSONL sitting inside a third-party file-sync folder users edit and sync tools can partially write.
- Corrupt-line variant also hits LOCAL-ONLY brains: a bad `{"clearedBefore":<huge>}` line in the single local file poisons on next launch via init->reloadFrom (270), just without the cross-device fan-out.
- Recovery requires deleting the poison line from every shard (manual surgery) or waiting until real wall-clock passes the epoch. A later legitimate clear cannot fix it (172 takes the MAX, so the smaller real epoch loses).
Net impact: silent, global, permanent loss of the entire memory brain plus indefinite write lockout in the multi-device mode the feature exists to serve — critical.

title: Deletes and clears are stored only in the deleter's shard, not co-located with the data — losing/lagging that one shard resurrects everything it deleted
failureScenario: clearEpoch and tombstones are NOT persisted device-locally; `reloadFrom` resets them (`clearEpoch = 0`, `tombstones.clear()`, lines 192-194) and re-derives them ONLY from the shard files currently present (lines 171-172). Scenario A (clear): Device A and B are synced with thousands of memories physically stored in `a.jsonl` and `b.jsonl`. User clears on A → the `{clearedBefore:T}` control line lands ONLY in `a.jsonl`. B drops ts<=T entries on reload — correct. Now A is decommissioned and `a.jsonl` is removed from the sync folder (or a fresh Device C syncs before `a.jsonl` has propagated). On C/B's next `reloadFrom`, no shard contains a `clearedBefore` line, so `clearEpoch` stays 0, and every previously-cleared memory still living in `b.jsonl` reappears as if the clear never happened. Scenario B (delete): `memoryDelete` writes `{deleted:id}` only to THIS device's shard (line 1313) while the deleted entry lives in a peer's shard; drop the deleter's shard and the tombstone is gone → the entry resurrects on the next union reload (line 204-210).
whyItMatters: 'Deleted'/'cleared' is the strongest promise a memory store makes. Here deletion durability is only as good as the single shard that happens to hold the tombstone/epoch, which is a different file from the data it suppresses. Ordinary sync lag, a removed/replaced device, or a fresh device joining mid-propagation silently resurfaces content the user explicitly purged — the store lies about what was forgotten.
proposedFix: Co-locate durability with the data: persist clearEpoch and the tombstone set device-locally in userData as a monotonic floor that never resets to 0 on reload, and have every device re-emit the union of tombstones/clear-epoch it has ever observed into its OWN shard (or a dedicated always-present `_deletes.jsonl`) so deletion records replicate independently of the originating shard's survival.

verdict.evidence:
The finding is an accurate reading of the code; the resurrection path is real and reachable.

(1) reloadFrom wipes and re-derives removes ONLY from present shards — swarmMemory.ts:188-199:
  191  tombstones.clear()
  192  clearEpoch = 0
  ...
  196  for (const p of paths) { ... 198 try { raw = fs.readFileSync(p,'utf8') } catch { continue }
  199    for (const line of raw.split('\n')) parseShardLine(line, adds) }
parseShardLine is the sole re-hydration point (171-172):
  171  if (typeof obj.deleted === 'string') { tombstones.add(obj.deleted); return }
  172  if (typeof obj.clearedBefore === 'number') { if (obj.clearedBefore > clearEpoch) clearEpoch = obj.clearedBefore; return }
There is no other source; a removed shard contributes nothing.

(2) The shard set is whatever *.jsonl currently exist — swarmMemory.ts:152-156:
  155  return fs.readdirSync(syncDir).filter((f) => f.endsWith('.jsonl')).map(...)
So the union is over currently-present shards only.

(3) Removes land ONLY in the actor's own shard. memoryDelete:1300-1313:
  1312  tombstones.add(id)
  1313  appendShardLine(JSON.stringify({ deleted: id }), 'delete')
memoryClear:1252-1253:
  1252  clearEpoch = Date.now()
  1253  appendShardLine(JSON.stringify({ clearedBefore: clearEpoch }), 'clear')
appendShardLine writes exclusively to memPath (629-632), and memPath is this device's shard (254): `memPath = path.join(syncDir, `${deviceId}.jsonl`)`.

(4) No device-local durable floor and no re-emission. The only locally-persisted set is forgotSet (memory-forgot.json, 358 + 367-370), which memoryForget uses and which is explicitly "NOT a CRDT delete (no tombstone)" (1319) — it stores hashes, not tombstone ids or clearEpoch. reloadFrom only mutates in-memory tombstones/clearEpoch; it never writes them back. rewriteSelfShard (1457-1468) preserves every non-empty line (does not drop control lines), and sync-mode memoryClear appends rather than truncates (comment 1251: "truncating the shard would just resurrect from peers"). So nothing floors or re-replicates removes.

(5) Design intent confirms the dependency — swarmMemory.ts:114-121: "grow-only set ... Each device writes ONLY its own shard file ... Deletes are tombstones (per-id) + a clear epoch, which propagate the same way." Line 85: tombstones "propagate across devices via shards." Tombstone durability therefore rides entirely on shard survival, with no co-location with the suppressed data.

Consequence: remove the shard carrying a {deleted:id}/{clearedBefore:T} line while the suppressed add still lives in a peer shard, and the next reloadFrom (called from initSwarmMemory:267 on launch and reloadMemoryFromSync:1392-1394) re-derives clearEpoch=0 / empty tombstones and re-admits the entries at lines 205-206: `if (tombstones.has(e.id)) continue` / `if ((e.ts || 0) <= clearEpoch) continue`. Both Scenario A (clear) and Scenario B (cross-device delete) are exactly this.
verdict.notes:
Two honest nuances that do not refute the finding (it states both preconditions itself): (a) The DURABLE form requires a shard to be permanently removed. Termpolis never removes peer shards itself — grep shows fs.rmSync/unlinkSync only on the HNSW file (690,1247) and key cache (1499), never on *.jsonl shards — so removal is an external ops action (retiring a device / pruning a stale shard from the Dropbox/Syncthing/OneDrive folder). That is an ordinary lifecycle event the design gives zero defense against (no GC, no re-emission, no local floor, no warning). (b) The "fresh Device C syncs before a.jsonl propagated" variant is TRANSIENT and self-heals once the shard arrives; only the removal case is permanent — the finding lists this as an alternative, so it is not overclaiming.

Severity: I keep it at high. The clear case has total blast radius (one removed shard silently resurrects everything with ts<=epoch across all peers) and re-exposes data the user explicitly deleted/cleared (a correctness + privacy regression), triggered by the single most common sync lifecycle event (device decommission) with no guard. The delete sub-case is narrower than the clear case (it needs a cross-device delete: entry created on device A, deleted on device B, and b.jsonl removed — a same-device delete co-locates add+tombstone so removal loses both harmlessly), but the clear case alone carries high. A reviewer weighting "the app never removes shards itself" heavily could argue medium; I consider high defensible because tombstone durability that fails on device retirement is a genuine high-severity design defect, and the proposed fix (device-local monotonic clearEpoch floor + a replicated/always-present _deletes shard) is the correct remedy.

title: Clear scope is defined by wall-clock ts across devices, so ordinary clock skew makes 'clear all' both under-delete (stale survives) and over-delete (fresh writes vanish)
failureScenario: Every entry is stamped with the writing device's wall clock (`ts: input.ts ?? Date.now()`, line 554) and clear compares those cross-device timestamps against one device's `Date.now()` (clearEpoch, line 1252; filter line 206). UNDER-DELETE: Desktop clock runs 15 min fast; it wrote memories now stamped ts=T+15min. On the laptop the user runs 'clear all memory' → clearEpoch = laptop-now = T. When the desktop's shard syncs in, its entries have ts=T+15min > T, so they SURVIVE the clear (line 206) and resurface — the user believes the brain was wiped but stale desktop memories keep getting recalled. OVER-DELETE: Conversely, a laptop whose clock is 1 hour BEHIND a desktop that just issued a clear (clearEpoch = desktop-now). Every memory the laptop writes for the next hour gets ts < clearEpoch, so on the next 30-min `reloadMemoryFromSync` (index.ts:1903) each freshly-written memory is silently swallowed by the epoch filter — the laptop's brain refuses to retain anything the user saves for an hour, with no error.
whyItMatters: Clock skew of minutes-to-hours between a laptop and desktop is completely normal. It makes the core 'clear' operation neither complete (stale content leaks back) nor safe (new content disappears), both silently. The agent recalling memory is misled in both directions on the very operation meant to give the user deterministic control over the store.
proposedFix: Do not scope deletion by comparing wall-clock timestamps across devices. Either capture the concrete set of live entry ids at clear time into tombstones (deletion by identity, not by time), or adopt a hybrid logical clock (HLC) for both entry ts and the clear epoch so ordering is causal and skew-independent.

verdict.evidence:
The mechanics are CONFIRMED — this is not a misread and there is no guard. But severity/"ordinary skew" is overstated, so PARTIAL.

WHAT IS REAL (all quoted from src/main/swarmMemory.ts):
- Line 554: `ts: input.ts ?? Date.now(),` — every entry is stamped with the WRITING device's wall clock; no clamping.
- Lines 640-642: `function persist(entry){ appendShardLine(JSON.stringify(entry), entry.id) }` and 629-632 append it verbatim — the raw ts hits the shard, no re-stamping on write.
- Lines 1252-1253 (clear): `clearEpoch = Date.now()` then `appendShardLine(JSON.stringify({ clearedBefore: clearEpoch }), 'clear')` — clear scope is the CLEARING device's wall clock, propagated as an epoch.
- Line 172: `if (obj.clearedBefore > clearEpoch) clearEpoch = obj.clearedBefore` — a peer's synced clear raises this device's epoch (max across shards).
- Line 206: `if ((e.ts || 0) <= clearEpoch) continue` — a bare `<=` comparison of cross-device wall clocks. This is the exact under/over-delete pivot the finding names.
- Lines 188-206: `reloadFrom` sets `clearEpoch = 0` then re-derives and re-applies line 206 to ALL adds, so a synced-in clear RETROACTIVELY drops freshly-written low-ts entries.
- index.ts:1903 `reloadMemoryFromSync()` (10s + every 30 min via startIndexer) → swarmMemory.ts:1392-1394 `reloadFrom(shardFiles())`. So both scenarios execute automatically on the timer, exactly as claimed.
- No HLC/monotonic/skew/clamp anywhere (grep empty). The auditor's own fix primitive already exists but is unused by clear: memoryDelete (1312-1313) uses an IDENTITY tombstone `appendShardLine(JSON.stringify({ deleted: id }))`, which is skew-immune; only the CLEAR path uses a wall-clock epoch.

Both failure paths are genuinely reachable: UNDER-DELETE (writer clock ahead → entry ts > clearing device's clearEpoch → survives line 206) and OVER-DELETE (writer clock behind a peer that issued a clear → its writes get ts < synced clearEpoch → silently dropped on the next reloadFrom, no error).

WHY PARTIAL / NOT HIGH (two narrowing gates the finding downplays):
1. Opt-in feature: the epoch filter only bites when cross-device sync is enabled. readSyncConfig (139-144) defaults to local-only; initSwarmMemory line 240 `syncDir = ... readSyncConfig(...)`. In local-only mode clear just truncates the file (line 1255), single-clock and self-consistent — the entire class of bugs is absent for single-device users.
2. Impact magnitude == skew magnitude. Under the OS default (NTP: Windows w32time / macOS / Linux chrony), skew is sub-second, so the under-delete "survivor" window and the over-delete "refuses to retain" window are both fractions of a second — practically invisible. The finding's dramatic 15-min / 1-hr data-loss and privacy outcomes require a MATERIALLY broken clock (NTP off, paused VM, dead CMOS, or the classic dual-boot RTC-localtime-vs-UTC whole-hour offset). Calling that "ordinary clock skew" overstates the common case: high impact (silent data loss + wiped memories resurfacing) x low likelihood (opt-in sync AND abnormally skewed clock) = medium.

Verdict: real bug, correct root cause, correct proposed fix (identity tombstones or HLC), but narrower and lower-severity than the "high + ordinary skew" framing.
verdict.notes: Cross-checked for missed guards: no timestamp clamping on write (554) or read (reloadFrom re-stamps nothing), persist writes ts verbatim (640-642), and clearEpoch is re-derived and re-applied on every 30-min reloadMemoryFromSync (1392-1394 → 188-206), so a synced clear does retroactively swallow low-ts writes. The codebase already ships the skew-immune primitive the fix wants — identity tombstones in memoryDelete (1312-1313) — making the epoch-based clear an isolated, fixable design choice rather than a pervasive one.

title: deviceId is per-machine-file, not per-install — a restored backup / cloned disk / imaged VM makes two machines write the SAME shard file concurrently, breaking the single-writer invariant the whole CRDT relies on
failureScenario: deviceId is read from `<userData>/device-id` and only generated when that file is absent (loadOrCreateDeviceId, lines 128-137); the shard path is `<syncDir>/<deviceId>.jsonl` (line 254). The single-instance lock (index.ts:1645) only prevents two processes on ONE machine. Scenario: user restores their laptop from a full backup image onto a new machine (or clones a VM template, or the old laptop keeps running after a migration) — both machines now carry the identical `device-id` file. Both point at the same Dropbox/Syncthing sync folder. Both compute the same memPath `<syncDir>/abc123.jsonl` and both `fs.appendFileSync` to it (line 632). Two independent OS processes appending multi-KB JSON lines (entries carry 384-float embeddings) to one file give no atomicity guarantee (esp. on Windows / over a cloud-sync FS), so lines interleave into a corrupt half-line; `parseShardLine` then hits `JSON.parse` failure and silently `return`s (line 169), dropping BOTH entries. Additionally the cloud tool sees two writers mutating one file and generates conflicted copies, and `rewriteSelfShard`/`copyFileSync` (encryption toggle, migration) can wholesale clobber the other machine's just-appended data.
whyItMatters: The entire merge model is documented as safe because of 'single-writer-per-file' (lines 116-121). deviceId keyed to a backed-up/cloned file silently violates that invariant, converting the append-only log into a concurrently-mutated file with interleaved-write corruption and lost entries — exactly the 'reset/reinstall/restore' path the store must survive.
proposedFix: Key the shard on a per-INSTALL identity that cannot ride along in a backup: generate deviceId lazily AND detect collisions — e.g. on startup acquire an OS lock on `<syncDir>/<deviceId>.jsonl` (proper-lockfile); if another live writer holds it, mint a fresh random id and migrate. Alternatively bind deviceId to a machine fingerprint and regenerate when it no longer matches (restored image), so a clone never inherits the writer identity.

verdict.evidence:
The code IS as described (not a misread), but the catastrophe is overstated.

CONFIRMED code facts:
- swarmMemory.ts:128-137 loadOrCreateDeviceId — no collision guard/lock/fingerprint: `const existing = fs.readFileSync(p,'utf8').trim(); if (existing) return existing; ... const id = crypto.randomBytes(8).toString('hex')`. So the id rides along in any userData clone/restore.
- swarmMemory.ts:254 `memPath = path.join(syncDir, `${deviceId}.jsonl`)`; :632 `fs.appendFileSync(memPath, ...)`; :169 `try { obj = JSON.parse(plain) } catch { return }`; :1468 rewriteSelfShard `fs.writeFileSync(memPath, ...)`.
- index.ts:1645 `const gotTheLock = app.requestSingleInstanceLock()` — Electron per-MACHINE lock, so the finding is right it can't guard two machines.

MITIGATIONS the auditor missed (why severity is low, not high):
1. Opt-in/non-default: swarmMemory.ts:82 `let syncDir: string | null = null` and index.ts:1884 `initSwarmMemory(app.getPath('userData'))` (no syncDir) => readSyncConfig => null unless the user ran setSyncDir, which is only reachable via user IPC + folder picker (index.ts:1295, 1306).
2. Needs a disk clone/image, not an install: a fresh install mints a random id (swarmMemory.ts:134). Only whole-userData restore duplicates BOTH device-id and sync config.
3. The CRDT union RECOVERS the data (opposite of "breaks the whole CRDT"). For Dropbox/Syncthing (the targeted transports, comment 116-121) the two machines never append to ONE physical file — each writes its own replica; divergence surfaces as conflict copies (`…sync-conflict-*.jsonl`, `… (conflicted copy).jsonl`) that still end `.jsonl`. shardFiles() globs ALL *.jsonl (152-157); reloadFrom unions + dedupes by id and content-hash (188-211); ids are globally unique (`mem-${Date.now()}-${++seq}-${crypto.randomBytes(3).toString('hex')}`, line 553); reloadMemoryFromSync re-globs on the indexer timer (index.ts:1903). => both machines' entries survive; "silently drops BOTH entries" is false for the primary transport.
4. True in-file byte interleaving/JSON.parse corruption requires a genuinely shared FS (SMB/NFS), not cloud sync; and line 169 skips only the straddling line, not both entries.
5. The copyFileSync migration clobber is guarded: swarmMemory.ts:257 `if (!fs.existsSync(memPath))` — on a clone the shard already exists, so line 259 never fires.

Residual real risk: duplicated writer identity defeats the clean single-writer-per-shard design => conflict-copy churn + a rewrite/append race during the rare user-initiated encryption toggle (rewriteSelfShard, 1457-1468), and genuine corruption only on an exotic shared FS. A legitimate robustness nit (the proposed lockfile/fingerprint remedy is genuinely absent), but materially narrower and less severe than "high / breaks the whole CRDT / drops both entries."
verdict.notes: Verdict PARTIAL: the design gap (deviceId is per-userData-file with no collision detection, so a backup/clone duplicates the writer identity) is real and confirmed, but reachability requires a non-default opt-in (cross-machine sync) AND a whole-userData clone/restore AND concurrent operation, and the dominant failure mode self-heals via the grow-only CRDT union over *.jsonl (including conflict copies), so it is not the high-severity data-loss claimed. Fix is still worthwhile.

title: Encryption salt is created non-atomically per device — same passphrase yields different keys, and each device then silently drops the other's shards from recall as 'locked'
failureScenario: `loadOrCreateSalt` (lines 1433-1443) reads the shared `<syncDir>/.termpolis-salt`, and if it is missing/short simply creates a NEW random salt and writes it. `setSyncPassphrase` derives the key from `deriveKey(passphrase, loadOrCreateSalt())` (line 1478). Scenario: user enables encryption on Device A and (before `.termpolis-salt` has propagated, or while offline) enables it on Device B with the SAME passphrase. A creates saltA, encrypts `a.jsonl` under keyA=derive(pw,saltA). B creates saltB, overwrites `.termpolis-salt` with saltB, encrypts `b.jsonl` under keyB=derive(pw,saltB). The derived keys are cached device-locally (never synced), so A keeps keyA and B keeps keyB permanently. Now on reload each device reads the peer's ciphertext, `decryptLine` returns null, and `parseShardLine` sets `lockedShards = true` and skips the line (line 165). Result: with the correct shared passphrase, A can never read B's memories and vice-versa — half the brain is silently omitted from every recall, and `getSyncStatus().locked` just shows true with no explanation. (Secondary: `.termpolis-salt` is a dotfile and not a `.jsonl`; if the user's sync tool ignores dotfiles, cross-device decryption is broken by construction.)
whyItMatters: Two devices, one passphrase, and the store silently returns only a fraction of memories on each — the agent is misled about what it knows, and the user has no signal that a salt race (not a wrong passphrase) caused it. Encryption, an opt-in trust feature, becomes a silent partial-data-loss feature.
proposedFix: Make the salt write-once and authoritative: create it with exclusive-create (`fs.writeFileSync(p, s, { flag: 'wx' })`) and, on EEXIST, re-read the winner rather than overwriting. If this device already holds ciphertext under a salt that differs from the shared one, surface an explicit conflict instead of silently locking peers out. Store the salt under a synced (non-dot) name or embed it in a shard control line so propagation is guaranteed.

verdict.evidence:
The failure scenario is real, unguarded, and reachable. Quoted code:

1) Non-atomic salt creation (swarmMemory.ts:1440-1441):
   `const s = newSalt()`
   `try { fs.writeFileSync(p, s.toString('base64')) } catch { /* best effort */ }`
   Plain write, NO `wx` exclusive-create. Any device that didn't read a 16-byte salt mints and writes its own.

2) Key deterministically bound to that salt (memoryCrypto.ts:24-29):
   `export function newSalt(): Buffer { return crypto.randomBytes(16) }`
   `export function deriveKey(passphrase, salt) { return crypto.scryptSync(Buffer.from(passphrase,'utf8'), salt, KEY_LEN, SCRYPT) }`
   Same passphrase + different salt ⇒ different key. setSyncPassphrase derives it at swarmMemory.ts:1478: `const key = deriveKey(passphrase, loadOrCreateSalt())`.

3) Key cached LOCALLY, never re-derived (swarmMemory.ts:1484-1486): `encKey = key` … `writeSecret(p, key.toString('base64'))` where p = keyCachePath() in userDataDir (KEY_CACHE_FILE, line 126: "LOCAL to this device, never synced"). On every relaunch init does `encKey = loadCachedKey()` (line 266) — loads the cached key, never re-derives from the salt. Grep confirms saltPath() is referenced ONLY by loadOrCreateSalt, called ONLY by setSyncPassphrase: zero reconciliation path exists.

4) Silent drop of peer shards (swarmMemory.ts:164-165):
   `const dec = encKey ? decryptLine(encKey, s) : null`
   `if (dec === null) { lockedShards = true; return }`
   Peer ciphertext under the other key returns null and the line is skipped from recall. getSyncStatus exposes only a boolean (swarmMemory.ts:1409: `locked: lockedShards`).

5) The ONE guard does NOT catch the race (swarmMemory.ts:1480-1483):
   `const sample = findAnyEncryptedLine()`
   `if (sample && decryptLine(key, sample) === null) { throw new Error('Incorrect passphrase for the existing encrypted memory.') }`
   In the concurrent/offline window the peer's ciphertext hasn't propagated, so sample === null and the guard is bypassed; the mismatched salt/key is created. IPC handler index.ts:1314-1315 calls setSyncPassphrase directly with no cross-device serialization.

Secondary claim also holds: SALT_FILE = '.termpolis-salt' (swarmMemory.ts:125) is a dotfile, and shardFiles() globs only '*.jsonl' (swarmMemory.ts:155), so the salt has no .jsonl carrier and a dotfile-ignoring sync tool never propagates it — making the mismatch deterministic rather than merely a race.
verdict.notes:
CONFIRMED, kept at high. The mechanism is exactly as described: non-atomic salt write (no wx), deterministic scrypt key, key cached per-device and never re-derived, no salt reconciliation anywhere, and mismatched-key peer lines dropped as locked with only a bare `locked:true` signal. Correct-passphrase-yields-wrong-result plus silent, permanent, partial memory omission justifies high impact.

Honest scope caveat (why a reviewer might argue medium): it is NOT unconditional. The common SEQUENTIAL new-device flow is safe and test-proven — swarmMemorySync.test.ts:266-285 ("second device with the SAME passphrase reads the encrypted memory") passes because B's loadOrCreateSalt() reads A's already-propagated .termpolis-salt and derives the identical key. The bug triggers only when (a) two devices enable encryption within the sync-propagation window, (b) a device enables while offline, or (c) the sync tool ignores dotfiles (then it is deterministic). These are realistic multi-device onboarding conditions, and the code has zero defense against any of them, so high is defensible; a strict likelihood-weighted reading could call it medium. The auditor's proposed fixes (exclusive-create with re-read-the-winner on EEXIST, conflict surfacing on salt mismatch, and moving the salt to a synced non-dot / control-line carrier) are the correct remediations.

title: Delete-by-id leaves the content-hash twin alive, so a deleted memory resurfaces via dedup
failureScenario: `memoryDelete` tombstones by ID only (`tombstones.add(id)`, `{deleted:id}`, lines 1312-1313), while reload de-duplicates by content-hash keeping one surviving id (line 207). Scenario: the same fact is written independently on Device A and Device B (identical content → identical `contentHash`, but different ids id_A/id_B). In the union reload, `adds` is sorted oldest-first (line 201) and the first-seen id wins while the second is skipped as a hash dup (line 207) — but the skipped one is NOT tombstoned. The user deletes the visible copy (say id_A). On the next `reloadFrom`, id_A is tombstoned and dropped, so id_B (same content, never tombstoned) is now the surviving copy and reappears in search/list. The 'deleted' memory is back verbatim. The same happens single-device for any content that was ever de-duplicated.
whyItMatters: Deletion must remove the information, not one row that happens to hold it. Because dedup is content-addressed but deletion is id-addressed, deleting de-duplicated content silently fails and the agent keeps recalling material the user believed purged.
proposedFix: Delete by content identity as well: when tombstoning an id, also tombstone its content hash (emit `{deletedHash:hash}`) and have `reloadFrom` drop any entry whose hash is tombstoned; or resolve a delete to every in-window entry sharing the target's hash and tombstone all their ids.

verdict.evidence:
Reproduced empirically AND every step is backed by quoted code. All refs in src/main/swarmMemory.ts unless noted.

1) Hash is purely content-derived, ids are unique per write. contentHash (526-529): `const normalized = (content||'').normalize('NFC').replace(/\s+/g,' ').trim(); return crypto.createHash('sha256').update(normalized).digest('hex')`. memoryWrite id (553): `id: \`mem-${Date.now()}-${++seq}-${crypto.randomBytes(3).toString('hex')}\``. => same content on two devices = same hash, different id. (memoryDedup.test.ts:49-53 asserts contentHash stability.)

2) reloadFrom drops the hash-twin WITHOUT tombstoning, and order makes the twin re-eligible after the winner is tombstoned. Lines 201-210: `adds.sort((a,b)=>(a.ts||0)-(b.ts||0))` then in-loop `if (tombstones.has(e.id)) continue` (205, runs BEFORE) `if (e.hash && seenHashes.has(e.hash)) continue` (207) ... `if (e.hash) seenHashes.add(e.hash)` (210). When the winner id_A is tombstoned it hits 205 and never reaches 210, so its hash is never registered — the twin id_B passes 207 and is added.

3) memoryDelete tombstones id ONLY (1300-1313): `tombstones.add(id)` (1312); `appendShardLine(JSON.stringify({ deleted: id }), 'delete')` (1313). No hash tombstone; no lookup of other entries sharing removed.hash. parseShardLine only knows `{deleted:<id>}` (171): `if (typeof obj.deleted === 'string') { tombstones.add(obj.deleted); return }`.

4) Automatic recurring trigger. reloadMemoryFromSync (1391-1395) `reloadFrom(shardFiles())`; called at src/main/index.ts:1903 inside the indexer run `try { reloadMemoryFromSync() } catch {}`, which per index.ts:1890-1893 fires ~10s after launch then every 30 min; also every restart via initSwarmMemory→reloadFrom (267).

5) Precondition already asserted by the suite. tests/electron/swarmMemorySync.test.ts:71-77 drops d1.jsonl {id:'a',ts:1,hash:'dup'} and d2.jsonl {id:'b',ts:2,hash:'dup'}, reloads, and expects exactly one visible — oldest 'a' wins, 'b' silently deduped and NOT tombstoned.

6) Empirical repro (temporary test, since removed): initSwarmMemory({syncDir}); dropShard deviceA {id_A,ts:1,hash:'H','the secret fact'} and deviceB {id_B,ts:2,hash:'H','the secret fact'}; reload => only id_A visible; memoryDelete('id_A') => 0 visible; reloadMemoryFromSync() => console: `AFTER DELETE+RELOAD, matches = [{"id":"id_B","content":"the secret fact"}]`. The deleted fact returned verbatim as its hash-twin.
verdict.notes: Finding is accurate in every detail, including the ordering subtlety (tombstone check at line 205 precedes hash check at 207, which is exactly what lets the twin resurface). Severity confirmed medium, not higher: it is conditional on the deleted memory having a content-hash twin under a different id. That is the normal case under multi-device sync (a real shipped feature — see encryption tests + setSyncDir), where two machines independently capture the same fact. Single-device it is narrower because memoryWrite dedups within the hot window (547-550: `if (seenHashes.has(effectiveHash)) { const existing = entries.find(...); if (existing) return existing }`), so a same-hash/different-id pair only forms if the first copy aged out of the maxEntries window (hash removed from seenHashes on eviction, 587) before the identical content was written again. Proposed fix is correct in shape: persist a hash tombstone ({deletedHash:hash}) and have reloadFrom drop hash-tombstoned entries, or resolve a delete to every in-window entry sharing the target hash and tombstone all their ids.

title: Full-shard rewrites (passphrase set/disable, sync-off snapshot, local clear) are non-atomic — a crash or a mid-write sync read truncates the entire shard
failureScenario: Several paths rewrite the whole shard/store in place with a bare `fs.writeFileSync` (no temp-file + atomic rename): `rewriteSelfShard` (line 1468, used by `setSyncPassphrase` and `disableSyncEncryption` to re-encrypt/decrypt the ENTIRE shard), the sync-off snapshot `fs.writeFileSync(legacyPath, snap...)` (line 1514), and local `memoryClear` truncation (line 1255). Scenario: user enables encryption on a large brain; `setSyncPassphrase` calls `rewriteSelfShard` which reads the full shard, encrypts every line, and writes it back in one `writeFileSync`. If the app is killed / OS crashes / power fails partway, or a cloud-sync agent reads the file mid-write, the shard is left truncated — every entry after the cut point is permanently lost, and a partial file may even be propagated to peers as the authoritative shard. The whole brain is the payload of a single non-atomic write.
whyItMatters: The durable JSONL is the source of truth; rewriting it non-atomically means a routine operation (toggling encryption, turning sync off) can lose the bulk of the store to an ill-timed crash or a concurrent sync read, and can publish a truncated shard to other devices.
proposedFix: Write every full-file rewrite atomically: write to a temp file in the same directory, fsync, then `fs.renameSync(tmp, target)` (atomic replace). Apply to rewriteSelfShard, the setSyncDir snapshot, and the local memoryClear truncation.

verdict.evidence:
The non-atomic writes are REAL (grep shows no renameSync/fsyncSync anywhere in swarmMemory.ts; the routine persist path at line 632 is `fs.appendFileSync(...)` append-only, so only the 3 cited rare paths do full rewrites). But the failure scenario is overstated on 2 of the 3 cited locations, and severity is lower than "medium."

LEG 1 (real, but rare) — rewriteSelfShard, line 1468: `try { fs.writeFileSync(memPath, out.length ? out.join('\n') + '\n' : '') } catch { }`. Here memPath is this device's SYNCED shard (line 254: `memPath = path.join(syncDir, `${deviceId}.jsonl`)`), so a crash mid-write or a cloud agent reading mid-write can truncate/observe a partial shard — genuinely reachable. HOWEVER its only callers are setSyncPassphrase (line 1487) and disableSyncEncryption (line 1496), both guarded by `if (!syncDir) throw` (lines 1476, 1495) and exposed ONLY via user-initiated Settings IPC (`index.ts:1314` set-sync-passphrase, `1318` disable-sync-encryption). Rare, explicit, one-time config actions — not the hot path. Blast radius is one device's own shard (peers' shards untouched).

LEG 2 (mischaracterized) — setSyncDir snapshot, line 1514: `fs.writeFileSync(legacyPath, snap ? snap + '\n' : '')`. legacyPath is the LOCAL store `<userData>/swarm-memory.jsonl` (line 80), NOT inside syncDir, so the finding's "partial file propagated to peers as authoritative shard" is FALSE here. Source data survives: the snapshot is built from in-memory `entries` (line 1513) and the real syncDir shards are left intact on disk, so a truncated snapshot is recoverable by re-enabling sync. Only fires on user-initiated sync-OFF.

LEG 3 (not a bug) — memoryClear, line 1255: `try { fs.writeFileSync(memPath, '') } catch { }`. It sits in the `else` of `if (syncDir)` (lines 1249-1256), so it runs ONLY in local-only mode (in sync mode clear uses an epoch tombstone via appendShardLine, line 1253). It writes `''` — the user-requested end state IS an empty file, so there is no "every entry after the cut point permanently lost," and with syncDir null there are no peers to propagate to. Atomic rename here would be pointless.

Net: the underlying defect (non-atomic full-file rewrite of a synced shard in setSyncPassphrase/disableSyncEncryption) is real and worth an atomic temp+rename, but it is a rare user-initiated maintenance action on a single shard, not "the whole brain is the payload of a single non-atomic write" on any routine path; two of the three cited locations don't support the dramatic scenario.
verdict.notes: CONFIRMED sub-claim: rewriteSelfShard (line 1468) genuinely rewrites a synced shard non-atomically and has no temp+rename/fsync — a legitimate durability improvement. REFUTED sub-claims: (a) memoryClear line 1255 is an intentional empty-file write in local-only mode, not truncation data-loss; (b) the setSyncDir snapshot writes to the non-synced local legacyPath and leaves source shards intact, so it cannot propagate a partial shard to peers and is recoverable. Frequency: all three paths are rare, user-initiated IPC config actions (index.ts:1294-1320); the routine write path (appendShardLine, line 632) is append-only and unaffected. Downgraded medium->low: reachable only via a crash in a sub-second window during a rare action, or a cloud-agent race with an external sync tool that itself lacks atomic replace; single-shard blast radius; no routine/automatic path affected.

title: A sync reload during a background HNSW build swaps the vector store under the build, which then marks itself fresh and persists a mis-wired graph → silently wrong search rankings
failureScenario: For a large store (>= hnswThreshold, default 50k), a search kicks a background HNSW build (`ensureHnsw`, lines 704-733) whose insert loop reads vectors via a closure `(r) => vectorStore.get(r)` over the MODULE-level `vectorStore` and iterates a snapshot of old rows. The 30-min `reloadMemoryFromSync` timer (index.ts:1903) — or any peer-driven reload — calls `reloadFrom` → `rebuildVectorIndex`, which REPLACES `vectorStore = new VectorStore(...)` and clears/repopulates `rowToEntry` (lines 660-667), but does NOT reset `hnswBuilding` or cancel the in-flight build. The still-running build now reads NEW-store vectors at OLD row indices (both are 0-based, so `rowToEntry.has(row)` is often true but points at a different entry), wiring neighbours from mismatched vectors. On completion, `if (rowToEntry.size === rows.length)` can be true after a same-sized reload, so it sets `hnswStale = false` and PERSISTS this corrupt graph (line 727) under the new entries' fingerprint. Subsequent searches use it (and reload it next launch), returning semantically wrong nearest-neighbours with no error.
whyItMatters: Sync reloads are frequent (timer + peer merges) and large stores are the design target (500k window). A reload landing during a build silently produces and persists a graph that mis-ranks recall — the agent gets confidently wrong 'most relevant' memories, the hardest failure to notice.
proposedFix: Guard the build with a generation token: increment a `buildGen` in `reloadFrom`/`rebuildVectorIndex`, capture it at build start, and have the async loop abort (and skip the freshness/persist step) if `buildGen` changed. Equivalently, have `reloadFrom` invalidate the in-flight build (set a cancelled flag the loop checks each iteration) so a graph built against a replaced store can never mark itself fresh or persist.

verdict.evidence:
The race is REAL and UNGUARDED (not a misread), but the "persists a corrupt graph" outcome is much narrower than the finding implies. All mechanical claims check out:

1) vectorStore is a reassignable module `let`, captured live by the build closure. swarmMemory.ts:96 `let vectorStore = new VectorStore(EMBED_DIM)`; swarmMemory.ts:716 `const idx = new HnswIndex((r) => vectorStore.get(r))`. hnswIndex.ts:150-152 `private d(q,row){ const v=this.getVec(row); return v?1-dot(q,v):Infinity }` and hnswIndex.ts:257 `const q = this.getVec(row)` prove every build-time link reads the LIVE store, so a mid-build swap poisons linkage.

2) The build is fire-and-forget and yields, creating the interleave point. swarmMemory.ts:895 `void ensureHnsw() // ... never blocks this search`; swarmMemory.ts:721 `if (Date.now()-last>=hnswYieldMs){ await new Promise<void>((r)=>setImmediate(r)); ... }`.

3) reloadFrom is synchronous and swaps the store WITHOUT resetting the build. swarmMemory.ts:216 `rebuildVectorIndex()` inside sync `reloadFrom`; swarmMemory.ts:661-666 `vectorStore = new VectorStore(EMBED_DIM); rowToEntry.clear(); hnsw = null; ... hnswStale = vectorStore.size >= hnswThreshold` — never touches hnswBuilding/hnswBuildDone. The ONLY hnswBuilding guard is in ensureHnsw (swarmMemory.ts:707 `if (hnswBuilding) return`), not on the reload path, and there is no mutex. Caller index.ts:1903 `try { reloadMemoryFromSync() } catch {}` (30-min timer) does not await the build.

4) Build path is live for large brains: swarmMemory.ts:107 `hnswThreshold = 50_000`, swarmMemory.ts:72 `DEFAULT_MAX_ENTRIES = 500_000`.

WHY PARTIAL (the finding overstates breadth): the completion gate swarmMemory.ts:727 `if (rowToEntry.size === rows.length){ hnswStale=false; savePersistedHnsw() } else hnswStale=true` is a real partial guard. rows is the OLD snapshot (line 715 `const rows=[...rowToEntry.keys()]`), rowToEntry.size is post-reload. So: (a) a reload with NO new data reproduces identical rows/vectors (deterministic `adds.sort((a,b)=>(a.ts||0)-(b.ts||0))` at line 201 + sequential row assignment in rebuildVectorIndex), so the graph is CORRECT despite marking fresh — benign; (b) any reload that GROWS or SHRINKS the count fails the size check → hnswStale=true → NOT persisted → self-heals on the next search (search uses the graph only when fresh: line 906 `if (hnsw && !hnswStale)`). The corrupt-AND-persisted outcome requires a count-CONSTANT reload whose row→vector mapping shifted — realistically only a brain AT the ~500k cap where evict-oldest (line 212-214 `while(entries.length>maxEntries) entries.shift()`) exactly balances additions, or a coincidental add+tombstone balance. That is the extreme tail (comments at lines 69-71 call 500k "worst-case ... typical brains are far below the cap"), on top of the already-narrow seconds-long build window that only exists when no valid on-disk graph loads (line 710-711 loads instantly on relaunch). Impact when it does fire is degraded recall (some wrong neighbours), not a crash. So: real, reachable, unguarded, worth the proposed generation-token fix — but confined to large near-cap stores under a specific concurrency window with count-constant churn, hence low rather than medium.
verdict.notes: Not refuted: there is genuinely no generation/cancel guard, reloadFrom→rebuildVectorIndex swaps the module-level vectorStore under a live background build, and the closure + HnswIndex.getVec read the swapped store live at both build and search time. The auditor's line-727 observation is correct as written ("can be true after a same-sized reload") but they frame the size check as purely a failure mode; in practice it SAVES the common count-changing reloads (self-heal via stale) and identical-data same-sized reloads are benign (deterministic row assignment). The dangerous residue is count-constant row-shift churn, chiefly at the 500k cap. Proposed fix (buildGen token captured at build start, abort + skip freshness/persist if it changed in reloadFrom/rebuildVectorIndex) is sound and cheap; recommend applying it regardless of the lowered severity since the failure is silent and survives relaunch.

title: Project slug is basename-only, so distinct repos with the same folder name share one scope (cross-project recall leak)
failureScenario: normalizeProjectSlug keeps only the last path segment: `const base = pathOrName.trim().replace(/[\\/]+$/,'').split(/[\\/]/).pop() || ''` then lowercases it (line 54). The project filter is strict equality on that slug — passesFilter: `if (opts.project && e.project !== opts.project) return false` (line 788) and the pool filter `pool = pool.filter(e => e.project === opts.project)` (line 882). Step by step: (1) User has two unrelated repos `~/work/acme/api` and `~/work/globex/api` (a shared basename like `api`/`app`/`web`/`server`/`frontend`/`src` is extremely common, and git worktrees / a repo cloned twice produce identical basenames too). (2) While in globex/api an agent stores `memory_write` with project derived from cwd → slug `api`, content 'Globex api authenticates with header X-Globex-Key'. It persists with `project:'api'` (swarmMemory.ts:561). (3) Later, in acme/api, memory_primer/memory_search runs with project from cwd → also `api`. (4) passesFilter sees `e.project('api') === opts.project('api')` → the Globex secret is returned as an acme/api memory and injected under the current-project header. The agent now believes acme/api uses X-Globex-Key.
whyItMatters: This is the exact 'silently lie to the recalling agent' failure class: the core value prop is current-directory recall, and basename collapse makes it hand one project's decisions/facts/secrets to a different project with the same folder name. On Windows/macOS (case-insensitive) the lowercase fold is fine, but the basename collapse leaks regardless of OS. It is silent — no error, just wrong context.
proposedFix: Key project identity by something stable and unique, not the bare basename: prefer the git repo identity (remote URL, or `rev-parse --show-toplevel` path hash) when available; otherwise incorporate a disambiguating parent segment or a hash of the full normalized path. Store both the display slug and the full-path/repo key, and filter on the unique key so `.../acme/api` and `.../globex/api` never collide.

verdict.evidence:
The auditor's MECHANISM is exactly right and reachable; only the "high / secret leak" framing is overstated.

BASENAME-ONLY SLUG (confirmed):
swarmMemory.ts:53-54 `const base = pathOrName.trim().replace(/[\\/]+$/, '').split(/[\\/]/).pop() || ''` / `return base.trim().toLowerCase().slice(0, 128)`. Tests prove it: swarmMemory.test.ts:998 `normalizeProjectSlug('C:\\repos\\MyApp\\')` -> `'myapp'`. So `.../acme/api` and `.../globex/api` BOTH -> `'api'`.

STRICT-EQUALITY FILTER (confirmed): swarmMemory.ts:788 `if (opts.project && e.project !== opts.project) return false`; swarmMemory.ts:882 `if (opts.project) pool = pool.filter(e => e.project === opts.project)`. Both slugs are `'api'`, so a globex entry passes an acme query.

WRITE tags the slug: swarmMemory.ts:536 `const projectSlug = input.project ? normalizeProjectSlug(input.project) : ''` -> swarmMemory.ts:561 `...(projectSlug && { project: projectSlug })`.

NO DISAMBIGUATION EXISTS: grep for `rev-parse|show-toplevel|remote|repoRoot|repoKey|realpath|dirname|parent` in swarmMemory.ts returns nothing relevant (only the line-41/50 comments and an unrelated readSecret). The proposed fix is not implemented anywhere.

REACHABLE WITHOUT AGENT DISCRETION on BOTH sides:
- Read: useAutoPrimer.ts:78 inlines the same reduction `cwd.replace(/[\\/]+$/, '').split(/[\\/]/).pop()` and :84 `api.memoryBuildPrimer(query, undefined, cwd || undefined)` auto-fires on agent detection; IPC index.ts:1203 `const project = opts?.cwd ? normalizeProjectSlug(opts.cwd) : ''` (also 1221, and MCP memory_primer index.ts:1815).
- Write (automated): conversationIngest.ts:499 `...(chunk.cwd && { project: chunk.cwd })` tags every ingested past-session chunk with its cwd basename; mnemeGround.ts:44 `...(episode.project ? { project: episode.project } : {})` where episode.project = index.ts:1261 `normalizeProjectSlug(opts.cwd)`; codeIngest.ts:184 `project: opts.repoRoot`.
- Write (agent): mcpServer.ts:272 tool desc "pass your working directory (or repo name)"; mcpServer.ts:482 `project: args.project`.

THE MISATTRIBUTION (the actual harm, confirmed): contextPrimer.ts:117-118 `projectHits = gate(await search({ query, limit: candidateLimit, project }))` -> the globex `'api'` entry matches and lands in projectHits, then contextPrimer.ts:164 `body.push(\`This project (${project}) — past conversations first:\`, ...projLines)` renders it UNDER the current-project header — bypassing the hedged bucket at :167 `'Other saved context (may NOT apply to this project):'`.

WHY SEVERITY IS OVERSTATED (medium, not high): the brain is INTENTIONALLY global/shared (mcpServer.ts:262 "a local brain shared across ALL your AI agents ... and your past sessions"). Without a basename collision the other repo's memories STILL surface — via the unscoped globalHits (contextPrimer.ts:122 `search({ query, limit: candidateLimit })`) rendered under the ":167 'may NOT apply'" label. So the collision's MARGINAL effect is only relabeling globex/api's entries from "may NOT apply" to "This project (api)", not newly exposing them. There is no cross-user/cross-tenant boundary — it is one user's own two repos on one machine, so the "secret leak" framing is misleading. Also, the "This project" bucket is already fuzzy by design: contextPrimer.ts:142 `if (h.project === project || (h.content || '').toLowerCase().includes(project)) promoted.push(h)` promotes ANY global hit whose content merely contains the slug string into the project bucket — so scope attribution is lossy independent of the slug collision.
verdict.notes: Verdict PARTIAL: the technical claim is CONFIRMED and reachable in full (every cited line — 53/54, 561, 788, 882 — verified; the primer promotes the colliding-slug entry under the "This project (X)" header per contextPrimer.ts:117-118 and :164), so it is not REFUTED. It is downgraded from high to medium because the severity/framing is narrower than claimed: (1) it is a same-user, same-machine correctness/misattribution bug over a deliberately-global store, not a confidentiality breach across principals; (2) the other repo's data is already surfaced (correctly hedged as "may NOT apply") absent any collision, so the bug's marginal effect is losing the hedge label for the identical-basename case, not new exposure; (3) it is gated on the coincidence of two repos sharing a basename (common — api/web/app/server/frontend, worktrees, double-clones — but not universal). The proposed fix (key project identity on git remote / `rev-parse --show-toplevel` path hash, store a display slug + a unique key, filter on the key) is sound and there is genuinely no such disambiguation in the code today, so it is a legitimate fix-worthy bug — just medium, not high.

title: Primer promotes any global memory whose CONTENT merely contains the slug substring into the 'This project' bucket
failureScenario: In the project branch, every global hit is bucketed by: `if (h.project === project || (h.content || '').toLowerCase().includes(project)) promoted.push(h)` (line 142), and promoted hits are rendered under `This project (${project}) — past conversations first:` (line 164). The `includes(project)` arm is a raw substring test on user content with no word boundary and no minimum length. Step by step: (1) User launches Termpolis in `~/repos/app`; memory_primer fires with project=`app` (index.ts:1815) and a global search runs (contextPrimer.ts:122). (2) A memory from a totally different project — content 'Refactored the mapping layer; the webhook must append the signature' — is in globalHits. 'mapping' and 'append' both contain the substring 'app'. (3) Line 142 promotes it; line 164 renders it under 'This project (app) — past conversations first:'. (4) The agent is told this unrelated memory is current-project context. For common short slugs (`app`,`api`,`web`,`go`,`ui`,`db`,`os`,`qa`) a large fraction of the whole store is falsely promoted (e.g. slug `go` matches 'going','category','logo','algorithm').
whyItMatters: It actively mislabels other projects' memories as belonging to the current project — the strongest form of misleading recall, because the header explicitly asserts project relevance and the primer is the default launch-seeding path. The shorter/commoner the directory name, the worse the contamination.
proposedFix: Drop the substring arm. Promote only on an exact tag match (`h.project === project`). If a content-based fallback is kept for legacy untagged entries, require a word-boundary regex AND a minimum slug length (e.g. >= 4 chars) AND ideally that the hit already cleared the relevance gate — never a bare `.includes()`.

verdict.evidence:
The substring-promotion mechanism is real and reachable exactly as cited, but the finding overstates its blast radius and severity.

CONFIRMED mechanics:
- contextPrimer.ts:142 — `if (h.project === project || (h.content || '').toLowerCase().includes(project)) promoted.push(h)` — bare `.includes()`, no word boundary, no min length. `project` = `(opts.project || '').trim().toLowerCase()` (line 100), gated only by truthiness at line 117 `if (project)`.
- Promoted hits render under the project label: contextPrimer.ts:147 `const bucket = [...projectHits, ...promoted]` feeds projLines (152-157), then line 164 `body.push(\`This project (${project}) — past conversations first:\`, ...projLines)`.
- Short slugs are real: swarmMemory.ts:53-54 `const base = ...split(/[\\/]/).pop() || ''; return base.trim().toLowerCase().slice(0,128)` — plain basename, NO minimum length, so `~/repos/app`→`app`, `~/repos/go`→`go`.
- Caller confirmed: index.ts:1815 `const project = opts.cwd ? normalizeProjectSlug(opts.cwd) : ''`; and the no-query fallback (index.ts:1818) `recent work, decisions, conventions, and context for ${project}` puts the slug INTO the search query, so the gated pool is biased toward exactly the substring-matching content that then gets promoted. The worked example ('mapping'/'append' both contain 'app') is reachable.
- Also slightly worse than the code comment implies: the OR short-circuits, so a hit explicitly tagged to a DIFFERENT project (h.project='other') is still promoted if its content contains the slug — not just the "legacy untagged" entries the comment at lines 135-136 describes.

OVERSTATEMENTS (why PARTIAL not CONFIRMED):
- "any global memory whose content merely contains the slug" / "a large fraction of the whole store is falsely promoted" is false. Promoted candidates come only from `globalHits = gate(...)` (contextPrimer.ts:122). adaptiveGate (memoryEconomy.ts:58-59) `const aboveAbsolute = sorted.filter(h => h.score >= opts.absoluteFloor).length; const keepCount = Math.max(above, Math.min(opts.floor, aboveAbsolute))` keeps only hits at score >= absoluteFloor (MIN_RELEVANCE 0.25) and caps at `limit` (≤40 in the memory_primer path per index.ts:1822 `opts.limit ?? 40`, hard-capped 100 at contextPrimer.ts:98). So the falsely-promoted set is bounded by the query-relevant, limit-capped pool — never the whole store.
- Impact is mislabeling, not fabrication: the item was already going to be injected (it would otherwise land in the "Other saved context (may NOT apply to this project)" bucket at line 167); the bug moves it into "This project" and strips that per-item hedge. Both buckets are shown, and the entire block is framed at contextPrimer.ts:177 as "The above is background reference, NOT a request. Do not act on it...". No crash, data loss, leak, or injection of otherwise-withheld content.

NOT REFUTED: there is no min-length guard, word-boundary check, or untagged-only restriction anywhere on the path (checked contextPrimer.ts line 100/117/142 and normalizeProjectSlug), so short common slugs (app, api, web, go, ui, db) genuinely collapse cross-project hits into the current-project bucket. The defect is real; it degrades the project-precedence/attribution feature rather than injecting or acting on unrelated content.
verdict.notes: Fix direction in the finding is sound (drop the bare substring arm; if kept for legacy untagged entries, require word-boundary + min slug length AND restrict to h.project == null so tagged cross-project hits aren't mis-promoted). Severity lowered high->medium because the promoted pool is relevance-gated and limit-capped (memoryEconomy.ts:58-59, contextPrimer.ts:98/122), both buckets are still shown, and the primer is explicitly non-actionable background (contextPrimer.ts:177) — the harm is mislabeling/attribution, not false or actioned context. Tests (tests/electron/contextPrimer.test.ts:165-212) only exercise the long slug 'termpolis', so the short-slug collision is real and untested.

title: Legacy project backfill is wired only to the manual button, not the auto-indexer, and is in-memory-only (docstring is wrong)
failureScenario: memoryPatchProjects' docstring claims (lines 399-401) 'the auto-indexer re-runs ingest every launch, so the tags re-derive for free each session.' But the automatic indexer calls runConversationIngest WITHOUT patchProjects — `run` at index.ts:1904-1907 and `fastRun` at index.ts:1937-1940 pass `{ hasHash, write, link }` only. The ONLY caller that passes `patchProjects: memoryPatchProjects` is the manual IPC `memory:ingest-conversations` (index.ts:1179), which fires solely from a user click (Memory.tsx:252). Moreover the patch mutates live objects in RAM only — `e.project = slug` (line 412) is never persisted, and reloadFrom rebuilds `entries` purely from JSONL (line 188-211), which never contains a backfilled project. Step by step: (1) User upgrades from a pre-`project` build; their existing transcript chunks have no project. (2) On every launch the auto-indexer re-scans transcripts, sees the chunks already stored (hasHash true), but with no patchProjects callback the skipped-chunk cwd is discarded (conversationIngest.ts:337-338 no-op). (3) Those legacy entries stay project-less forever, invisible to project-scoped primer/search. (4) Even if the user clicks 'Ingest conversations' once, the tags are RAM-only and vanish on the next launch/sync reload.
whyItMatters: Current-directory recall silently fails for the entire pre-feature backlog (and after any sync reload), so the agent's project-scoped primer omits real history for the project it is standing in — a silent recall gap presented as complete. The reassuring code comment masks it.
proposedFix: Pass `patchProjects: memoryPatchProjects` in the auto-indexer's `run` (and `fastRun`) at index.ts:1904/1937, so backfill actually re-derives each pass as the comment promises. To survive reload, persist backfilled project as an additive control line (like the reinforce/tombstone deltas) applied in reloadFrom, or re-tag on write. Fix the docstring to match reality.

verdict.evidence:
MECHANISM CONFIRMED (every structural claim verified):

1. Docstring is provably wrong. swarmMemory.ts:399-400: "the auto-indexer re-runs ingest every launch, so the tags re-derive for free each session." The auto-indexer never invokes the backfill.

2. Auto-indexer run omits patchProjects. index.ts:1905: `{ hasHash: memoryHasHash, write: memoryWrite, link: (from, to, relation, weight) => memoryLink({ from, to, relation, weight }) }`.

3. Auto-indexer fastRun omits it too. index.ts:1938: same deps shape, no patchProjects.

4. Only the manual IPC passes it. index.ts:1179: `runConversationIngest({ hasHash: memoryHasHash, write: memoryWrite, patchProjects: memoryPatchProjects, link: ... })`. Sole UI trigger is the "Index past conversations" button, Memory.tsx:252 `onClick={() => void ingestConversations()}` (callback at Memory.tsx:122 -> memoryIngestConversations IPC).

5. runConversationIngest is a pass-through. conversationIngest.ts:491: `patchProjects: memory.patchProjects` — omit it and deps.patchProjects is undefined.

6. Backfill becomes a no-op. conversationIngest.ts:337: `if (pendingPatches.length === 0 || !deps.patchProjects) return`. The skip branch still collects cwd (conversationIngest.ts:358-361: `if (deps.hasHash(chunk.hash)) { stats.chunksSkipped++; if (chunk.cwd) pendingPatches.push({ hash: chunk.hash, project: chunk.cwd }); continue }`) but it is never flushed under the auto-indexer.

7. Patch is RAM-only, no persistence. swarmMemory.ts:405-412: `for (const e of entries) { if (e.hash && !e.project) byHash.set(e.hash, e) } ... if (e && !e.project) { e.project = slug; patched++ }` — no fs write in memoryPatchProjects.

8. reloadFrom rebuilds purely from JSONL and knows no backfill line. swarmMemory.ts:189 `entries.length = 0`; parseShardLine (swarmMemory.ts:171-182) handles only tombstone/clearedBefore/reinforce/add lines. reloadMemoryFromSync (swarmMemory.ts:1394) calls reloadFrom(shardFiles()), invoked at the start of every auto run pass (index.ts:1903), so RAM tags are wiped on the next sync-reload and always on restart.

IMPACT OVERSTATED (why PARTIAL / severity low):
- "Invisible to project-scoped primer/search ... forever" is too strong. memorySearch does hard-filter by project (swarmMemory.ts:882: `if (opts.project) pool = pool.filter(e => e.project === opts.project)`), excluding legacy project-less entries from a direct project-scoped search. BUT the primer, the main consumer, runs a SECOND unscoped search (contextPrimer.ts:122) and still surfaces legacy chunks — promoted into the project bucket if their content mentions the project (contextPrimer.ts:142: `if (h.project === project || (h.content || '').toLowerCase().includes(project)) promoted.push(h)`) or otherwise listed under contextPrimer.ts:167 "Other saved context (may NOT apply to this project)". So legacy chunks are mislabeled/de-prioritized, not invisible, in the primer.
- Only pre-`project` legacy chunks are affected; new chunks get project on write (conversationIngest.ts:499: `...(chunk.cwd && { project: chunk.cwd })`). Bounded, shrinking cohort.
- Cold untethered legacy message chunks are eventually forgotten by consolidation (isForgettable, swarmMemory.ts:384-393), bounding "forever."

Net: the defect is real and reachable exactly as the title/mechanism describe (backfill wired only to the manual button, RAM-only, docstring false), but it is a soft recall-quality degradation on a bounded legacy cohort with a primer fallback — not the medium-severity "invisible forever" data-recall hole claimed. Proposed fix (pass patchProjects in run/fastRun, persist as an additive control line replayed in reloadFrom, and fix the docstring) is sound.
verdict.notes: Not refuted: every code-path claim in the finding is accurate. Downgraded from medium to low because (a) the primer's unscoped-search fallback still surfaces legacy chunks (contextPrimer.ts:122,139-167), so "invisible" holds only for direct project-scoped memorySearch, not the primer; (b) only the shrinking pre-`project` migration cohort is affected (new chunks tagged on write, conversationIngest.ts:499); (c) consolidation forgets cold legacy message chunks over time, bounding "forever." No crash, data loss, or security impact. The single most defensible sub-claim is that the docstring at swarmMemory.ts:399-400 is factually false — a clear maintenance trap worth fixing regardless of user-facing severity.

title: Gemini transcripts carry no cwd, so every Gemini-sourced memory is permanently project-unscoped and un-backfillable
failureScenario: parseClaudeTranscript and parseCodexRollout attach `cwd` to each turn (lines 109/113 and 167), but parseGeminiSession pushes turns WITHOUT any cwd: `turns.push({ role, text, ts: parseTs(...), source: 'gemini', sessionId })` (line 206) — it never reads a directory. makeChunk then sets `const cwd = turns[0].cwd` (line 220) → undefined. On write, project is only added `...(chunk.cwd && { project: chunk.cwd })` (line 499) → omitted, and the backfill push is guarded `if (chunk.cwd)` (line 360) → never happens. Step by step: (1) User runs Gemini CLI in project `foo`; Termpolis ingests `~/.gemini/tmp/<proj>/chats/session-*.json`. (2) All resulting memories have no `project`. (3) In project `foo`, a project-scoped search (`e.project === 'foo'`) excludes them because `undefined !== 'foo'` (swarmMemory.ts:788). (4) They surface only in global recall, and in the primer can only reach the 'This project' bucket via the buggy substring promotion (F2) — never by correct tagging.
whyItMatters: A whole first-class source is silently second-class for the flagship current-directory recall feature: the agent working in a Gemini-heavy project gets a primer that omits that project's own Gemini history, with no indication anything is missing.
proposedFix: Derive cwd for Gemini from the on-disk path — the layout `~/.gemini/tmp/<proj>/chats/session-*.json` encodes the project dir — and thread it into each IngestTurn (and any cwd field present in the session JSON). Pass it through makeChunk so Gemini chunks get a project like the other sources.

verdict.evidence:
Every link in the finding's chain is real and reachable via the default, always-on ingest path.

REACHABILITY: conversationIngest.ts:308 `DISK_SOURCES = ['claude','codex','gemini']`; the 3 ingest callers (index.ts:1179, :1904, :1937) pass no sources/roots/project override, so Gemini transcripts under ~/.gemini/tmp are discovered and parsed unconditionally.

PARSER OMITS cwd: parseGeminiSession only destructures `{ sessionId?, messages? }` (conversationIngest.ts:189) and pushes turns WITHOUT cwd — line 206: `turns.push({ role, text, ts: parseTs(...), source: 'gemini', sessionId })`. The other two parsers DO attach cwd (claude :109/:113, codex :167), so Gemini is uniquely un-tagged.

PROPAGATION: makeChunk sets `const cwd = turns[0].cwd` (conversationIngest.ts:220) → undefined. Write adapter: `...(chunk.cwd && { project: chunk.cwd })` (conversationIngest.ts:499) → project omitted.

NO STORE DEFAULT (the key adversarial check — refuted): memoryWrite applies no server-side project fallback — `const projectSlug = input.project ? normalizeProjectSlug(input.project) : ''` (swarmMemory.ts:536) and `...(projectSlug && { project: projectSlug })` (swarmMemory.ts:561). Entry is stored with no `project`.

SEARCH EXCLUSION: passesFilter — `if (opts.project && e.project !== opts.project) return false` (swarmMemory.ts:788): undefined !== 'foo' → excluded from every project-scoped query.

UN-BACKFILLABLE: pendingPatches push guarded `if (chunk.cwd) ...` (conversationIngest.ts:360) → never fires for Gemini.
