DOWNSTREAM PRIMER: global search is unscoped (contextPrimer.ts:122) so Gemini memories DO appear globally, but project promotion is `if (h.project === project || content.includes(project))` (contextPrimer.ts:142) — a project-undefined Gemini hit reaches the "This project" bucket only via the substring branch, else it lands under "Other saved context (may NOT apply to this project)" (:167). Exactly the finding's step (4).

SUPPORTING: test fixture tests/electron/conversationIngest.test.ts:80-87 shows the Gemini JSON carries `projectHash: 'abc123'` (a hash, no cwd path), and normalizeProjectSlug (swarmMemory.ts:51-54) returns a lowercased last-path-segment slug — so the proposed path-derivation fix would produce a hash that still would not match a real slug like 'foo'. The defect is confirmed; the fix is under-specified but that does not narrow the defect.
verdict.notes: CONFIRMED and reachable via the default background indexer (index.ts:1904/1937) — no setting gates Gemini out. Severity held at medium: it is a permanent, silent relevance regression in a first-class feature (project-scoped primer / MCP recall), affecting an entire source. Borderline-low arguments (which I weighed but did not adopt): memories are NOT lost — they remain in global semantic recall (contextPrimer.ts:122) and can still reach the project bucket when content mentions the project name (contextPrimer.ts:142); the impact is scoping precision, not availability; and it is confined to Gemini, a source the code repeatedly labels best-effort/undocumented while Claude and Codex are unaffected. One correction to the finding's remediation (not the defect): the on-disk `<proj>` dir and the JSON `projectHash` are HASHES, not the readable cwd, and normalizeProjectSlug (swarmMemory.ts:51-54) produces a last-segment slug — so simply threading the path through would tag Gemini entries with a hash that still would not match a normal project-scoped search; a real fix needs Gemini's projectHash→path reverse map (or a projectHash-aware match). This makes the defect marginally harder to fix than the finding implies, but does not reduce its reality or reachability.

title: Curated agent memory_write defaults to unscoped: project is only set if the model remembers to pass it, so high-value decisions miss project recall
failureScenario: The MCP memory_write handler forwards `project: args.project` verbatim (mcpServer.ts:482) and the IPC memory_write passes `project: input.project` (index.ts:1777) — there is no fallback to the calling terminal's cwd. The schema only *asks* the model to 'pass your working directory' (mcpServer.ts:272). Ingested transcript chunks DO get a cwd-derived project (conversationIngest.ts:499), but agent-authored decisions/facts/notes do not unless the model opts in every call. Step by step: (1) In project `foo`, the agent calls memory_write kind='decision' content='We chose Postgres over SQLite for foo' and omits `project` (common — it's optional). (2) It stores with no project (swarmMemory.ts:536,561 skip it). (3) On the next launch in `foo`, memory_primer scopes to `foo`; the strict filter excludes the decision (undefined !== 'foo'). (4) The decision is relegated to the 'Other saved context (may NOT apply to this project)' bucket (contextPrimer.ts:167) — i.e. the project's own decision is labeled as possibly-not-its.
whyItMatters: Scoping is inverted: low-value bulk transcript chunks are reliably project-tagged while the highest-value curated knowledge usually isn't, so project-scoped recall systematically under-serves and even mislabels the very memories it exists to resurface.
proposedFix: At the server/IPC boundary, default `project` from the calling terminal's cwd when the agent omits it (the app already knows the terminal's directory). Keep the explicit arg as an override. This makes curated writes scoped-by-default and consistent with ingested chunks.

verdict.evidence:
WRITE-SIDE MECHANISM = CONFIRMED (no cwd default anywhere on the agent write path):
- mcpServer.ts:476-482 `case 'memory_write': return await handlers.memoryWrite({ agentId: args.agentId, kind: args.kind, content: args.content, tags: args.tags, taskId: args.taskId, project: args.project })` — forwarded verbatim.
- index.ts:1769-1777 IPC handler: `memoryWrite: async (input) => { ... await memoryWrite({ ... project: input.project }) }` — verbatim, no fallback.
- swarmMemory.ts:536 `const projectSlug = input.project ? normalizeProjectSlug(input.project) : ''` and :561 `...(projectSlug && { project: projectSlug }),` — when the model omits project the entry gets NO project field.
- mcpServer.ts:274 `required: ['agentId', 'content'],` (project is optional); :272 description only *asks* the model to "pass your working directory".
- Asymmetry is real: conversationIngest.ts:499 `...(chunk.cwd && { project: chunk.cwd }), // store normalizes to a slug` — ingested chunks ARE cwd-scoped; index.ts:1984-1990 auto-ingest of swarm events also omits project. No agent-facing write path injects project.

CONSEQUENCE = SOFTER / NARROWER than claimed (two guards the finding understated):
- contextPrimer.ts:142 `if (h.project === project || (h.content || '').toLowerCase().includes(project)) promoted.push(h)` — a project-less entry whose CONTENT mentions the project slug is PROMOTED into the project bucket, not relegated. normalizeProjectSlug (swarmMemory.ts:51-55) makes the slug the lowercased cwd basename, so the finding's own example content "We chose Postgres over SQLite for foo" (slug 'foo') is promoted — contradicting its step (4).
- contextPrimer.ts:158-167: entries that DO fall to `others` are still rendered (`otherLines.push(line)`) and emitted under `'Other saved context (may NOT apply to this project):'`. They are mislabeled, NOT excluded from the digest — so the title's "miss project recall" overstates the primer path.
- The only HARD exclusion is swarmMemory.ts:882 `if (opts.project) pool = pool.filter(e => e.project === opts.project)`, which bites only when the READER passes project to memory_search — symmetric optionality; a project-less search still returns the decision.
verdict.notes: Verdict PARTIAL, corrected severity low (finding said medium). The write-side defect is genuine and reachable: an agent can call memory_write with just the required agentId+content (kind='decision') and the decision is stored with no project field, while transcript ingestion auto-derives project from cwd (conversationIngest.ts:499) — a real, avoidable asymmetry, and the fix (default project from the terminal cwd at the mcpServer/IPC boundary) is reasonable. What drops severity: (1) the launch primer IS project-scoped by default (buildPrimerPointer/useAutoPrimer.ts:29-31 -> index.ts:1815), but the primer pulls project-less entries via its UNSCOPED globalHits pass (contextPrimer.ts:122) and then either PROMOTES them by content-mention (line 142 — which catches the finding's own example) or shows them under a "may NOT apply" caveat (line 167) — it does not lose them; (2) full exclusion only occurs on an opt-in project-scoped memory_search (swarmMemory.ts:882). So the true residual harm is limited to: decisions whose text does NOT contain the cwd basename get a softer "may NOT apply to this project" label in the primer, and are missed by project-scoped searches. That is a real labeling/recall-quality nick, but materially milder and less certain than the "high-value decisions miss project recall" headline. Minor aside: the self-record guidance (useAutoPrimer.ts:38-40) says to write "tagged to this project" — tags do not populate the `project` field the filters check, so even a compliant model may still write unscoped, reinforcing the underlying gap without changing the severity.

title: cwd is captured first-wins per transcript and applied to all chunks, mis-tagging sessions that span directories
failureScenario: Claude parsing latches the first cwd and never updates it: `if (!cwd && typeof obj.cwd === 'string') cwd = obj.cwd` (line 95); Codex takes cwd only from the one session_meta payload (line 146). makeChunk then stamps ALL chunks of the transcript with `turns[0].cwd` (line 220), discarding any later, differing cwd. Step by step: (1) A session's transcript records work first under `~/repos/foo` and later under `~/repos/bar` (resumed elsewhere, `/add-dir`, or a tool that changes the recorded cwd). (2) Every chunk — including the bar work — is tagged project=`foo`. (3) Recall in `bar` (project=`bar`) misses that work entirely, while recall in `foo` surfaces bar's memories as foo's. Related fragility: a Codex rollout read mid-write before its session_meta line is flushed yields cwd=undefined for the whole file, leaving those memories unscoped like the Gemini case.
whyItMatters: A single collapsed cwd both loses recall for the true project and leaks it into the first one — the same misattribution pattern as the ts-at-ingestion bug, but on the project axis. It corrupts scoping precisely for the power-user sessions that move between repos.
proposedFix: Preserve per-turn cwd (already present on IngestTurn) and split chunks on cwd change so each chunk carries the cwd of its own turns; have makeChunk use the chunk's turns rather than always turns[0]. For Codex, fall back to the file path or a later cwd if session_meta is absent.

verdict.evidence:
CORE MECHANISM IS REAL (exact code, conversationIngest.ts):
- L95 `if (!cwd && typeof obj.cwd === 'string') cwd = obj.cwd` — Claude cwd latches first-wins, never updated.
- L109/113 every turn is pushed with that single `cwd` variable, so ALL turns of a file carry the first-seen cwd.
- L220 `const cwd = turns[0].cwd` — makeChunk therefore stamps every chunk with the first cwd (all turns are identical anyway).
- L499 `...(chunk.cwd && { project: chunk.cwd })` writes it as the entry's project.
- swarmMemory.ts:53 normalizes to the lowercased basename; swarmMemory.ts:788 `if (opts.project && e.project !== opts.project) return false` and :882 `pool = pool.filter(e => e.project === opts.project)` make project a HARD recall filter. So a mis-tag really does mis-scope recall.

REACHABILITY IS CONFIRMED EMPIRICALLY — I scanned the user's real transcripts (~/.claude/projects). 14 of 1023 .jsonl files contain >1 distinct cwd whose BASENAMES differ within a single file, e.g.:
  79504e90-...jsonl: first cwd C:\Users\DavidEngelhart (slug 'davidengelhart'), later C:\Users\DavidEngelhart\repos\MSI-PAS-CORE and ...\repos\termpolis → first-wins tags ALL that session's chunks 'davidengelhart', so the termpolis/msi-pas-core work is mis-scoped.
  668cacb6-...: 'davidengelhart' + 'termpolis-web'; 4294bcc6-...: 'repos'+'msi-pipelines'+'msi-pas-core'; 9b43a995-...: 'memex'+'a[dato]m'. So the "session spans directories" premise genuinely occurs. The wrong-attribution half ("recall in foo surfaces bar's memories as foo's") is REAL and UNMITIGATED: contextPrimer.ts:164 places the project-scoped (mis-tagged) hits under the literal "This project (foo) — past conversations first:" bucket.

WHY IT IS NARROWER / LESS SEVERE THAN CLAIMED (→ PARTIAL, low):
1. The "recall in bar misses that work ENTIRELY" claim is overstated for the primary path. The auto-primer (the shipping default, invoked by memory-primer-hook.cjs and index.ts:1814) calls buildContextPrimer, which runs a project search (contextPrimer.ts:118) AND an UNSCOPED global search (L122), then promotes any global hit whose content mentions the project or is tagged for it (L142 `if (h.project === project || (h.content||'').toLowerCase().includes(project))`) into the project bucket, dumping the rest under "Other saved context (may NOT apply)" (L167). Since a termpolis chunk almost always contains the word "termpolis", it is typically still surfaced (possibly mislabeled/deprioritized), not lost. Complete invisibility only holds for a direct project-scoped memory_search call (index.ts:1794 → swarmMemory:882), which has no fallback.
2. Incidence is ~1% of transcripts (14/1023), and after basename normalization several of those are harmless same-repo subdirectories (e.g. msi-pas-core vs its 'scripts'/'.sweep/tick-...' subdir, not a different project). Genuinely cross-repo spans are ~5-6 files. Only turns AFTER the cwd change are mis-tagged; the first project's turns are correct.
3. The Codex half of the finding is essentially unreachable. I scanned ~/.codex/sessions: 14/15 rollouts have session_meta and in ALL 14 it is the FIRST line (0 rollouts missing it). session_meta is written at rollout creation, so a mid-write incremental read still sees it; and readFile ingests the whole file with idempotent hashing, so a later full read corrects any partial. Moreover Codex records only the one session_meta cwd (no per-message cwd), so its "spans directories → later cwd discarded" scenario doesn't even apply — there is no later cwd to discard. An undefined-cwd Codex/Gemini chunk is merely left unscoped (project omitted at index.ts:499), which for Gemini is the accepted baseline (parseGeminiSession never sets cwd at all, L206) and remains reachable via global search.

NET: the defect (first-wins cwd mis-tagging multi-directory Claude sessions) is real, reachable, and demonstrated in live data, and produces genuine wrong-project attribution. But the headline "misses that work entirely" is mitigated in the main recall path, the Codex sub-claim is unreachable, and real-world incidence is ~1% — so medium overstates it. Corrected severity: low.
verdict.notes: Proposed fix is directionally right (split chunks on cwd change; use the chunk's own turns) but note makeChunk ALREADY uses the chunk's turns[0], not the transcript's global turns[0] — the real root cause is the parser latching cwd at conversationIngest.ts:95 (Claude) and stamping every turn with it (L109/113), so per-turn cwd must be preserved in the parser, not just in makeChunk. The Codex fallback part of the fix is low-value since Codex records only one cwd and session_meta is reliably the first line. A cheap additional win: since Claude's on-disk project directory name already encodes the launch cwd, the ingester could derive project from the file path as a stable fallback.

title: memory_search and memory_primer never drop superseded memories — only memory_graph does, so a decision the agent explicitly marked obsolete resurfaces as the top/leading recall
failureScenario: 1) Agent stores decision D1 'Use REST for the sync API' (memory_write → id mem-A). 2) Later it stores D2 'Switched sync API to gRPC; REST is deprecated' (id mem-B) and, exactly as the memory_link tool tells it to ('a decision that supersedes an older one'), calls memory_link{from:mem-B, to:mem-A, relation:'supersedes'}. 3) A new session calls memory_search{query:'sync API transport'} or loads memory_primer. memorySearch (swarmMemory.ts:862-1025) scores/ranks/gates/diversifies but NEVER calls filterSuperseded — which is imported (line 12) yet used at only one site, memoryGraphQuery line 1134. buildContextPrimer (contextPrimer.ts:95-181) also never calls it. 4) D1 (higher cosine to 'REST', or simply both present) is returned to the agent — often ranked at or above D2 — with no 'superseded' marker. The agent acts on the deprecated REST decision. memoryGraphQuery's own comment (line 1132-1133) 'never hand back a memory that a later one supersedes' proves the guarantee exists ONLY for graph traversal, not for the two primary recall paths.
whyItMatters: The memory_link tool actively solicits supersedes/superseded-by edges and implies they keep stale answers from resurfacing; but the paths agents actually recall through (search, primer) ignore them. The brain silently presents replaced knowledge as current — the exact 'resurface stale content as fresh' failure the audit targets, and it worsens as the store grows.
proposedFix: Apply the existing filterSuperseded(hits, getAllEdges()) at the end of memorySearch (before searchCache.set) and inside buildContextPrimer's gate, or at minimum tag superseded hits with a '⚠ SUPERSEDED by <id>' label in renderLine the same way the stale-file guard works. supersededIds/filterSuperseded are already implemented in mnemeGraphLogic.ts.

verdict.evidence:
filterSuperseded is imported at swarmMemory.ts:12 but called at exactly ONE site — swarmMemory.ts:1134 `const active = filterSuperseded(out, getAllEdges())` inside memoryGraphQuery (the memory_graph tool), guarded by the comment at 1132-1133 "P3: never hand back a memory that a later one supersedes — the 'no confusion as the store grows' guarantee". A repo-wide grep confirms no other src call site.

memorySearch (swarmMemory.ts:862-1025): full read; ends at 1023 `searchCache.set(cacheKey, result)` / 1024 `return result` with NO supersession filter. The default diversify path (988-1003) only does gateByScore + mmrRerank (relevance/wording heuristics), not supersession.

title: memory_write silently de-dupes by content and throws away the new call's project/tags/taskId, so project-scoped recall silently misses the fact the agent believes it just filed
failureScenario: 1) A transcript chunk 'Use pnpm, not npm, in this repo' was ingested earlier with no project (or project='other-repo'). 2) Agent working in C:/repos/foo calls memory_write{content:'Use pnpm, not npm, in this repo', project:'C:/repos/foo', tags:['tooling']}. The MCP handler (index.ts:1769-1777) forwards project verbatim. 3) memoryWrite computes effectiveHash = contentHash(content) (NFC + whitespace-collapsed, case-preserved), sees seenHashes.has(hash) is true, and at line 548-549 returns the pre-existing entry, skipping persist + index + the projectSlug assignment entirely. The agent gets back id/success and assumes the note is now filed under 'foo' with tag 'tooling'. 4) A later memory_search{query:'package manager', project:'C:/repos/foo'} filters pool with e.project === 'foo' (line 882) — the note has project undefined/'other-repo', so it is NOT returned. The current-directory-priority promise in the tool description ('pass your working directory ... so the memory is recalled with current-directory priority', mcpServer.ts:272) silently fails.
whyItMatters: The write reports success while discarding the very metadata that governs recall scope, and the agent has no way to know its association was dropped. Two agents (or a re-ingest) writing the same sentence race to own its project tag, and whoever loses is invisible under project-scoped search — a silent completeness hole in the product's headline 'current-directory recall'.
proposedFix: On a dedup hit, backfill missing metadata onto the existing entry before returning it: if existing.project is empty set it to projectSlug, union tags, adopt taskId (mirrors memoryPatchProjects). And/or return a { deduped: true, mergedInto: existing.id } flag so the agent knows its write collapsed into another entry rather than being stored as-specified.

verdict.evidence:
The dedup-drops-metadata CODE is real (swarmMemory.ts:546-549): `const effectiveHash = input.hash || contentHash(content); if (seenHashes.has(effectiveHash)) { const existing = entries.find(e => e.hash === effectiveHash); if (existing) return existing }` — returns the pre-existing entry, skipping the projectSlug/tags/taskId assignment at lines 558-561. Project recall is a hard filter with no fallback (swarmMemory.ts:882-883): `if (opts.project) pool = pool.filter(e => e.project === opts.project)` then `if (pool.length === 0) return []`. Write (line 536) and search (line 869-871) both `normalizeProjectSlug`, so a mis-projected entry is truly unrecallable under the intended project.

HOWEVER the finding's specific scenario — a previously INGESTED TRANSCRIPT CHUNK colliding with the agent's direct write — is UNREACHABLE, because the two hashes are computed differently and cannot be equal:
- Ingestion hash (conversationIngest.ts:222-225): `crypto.createHash('sha256').update(`${source}${sessionId ?? ''}${text}`)` where `source` is always non-empty (conversationIngest.ts:218/206, e.g. 'gemini') and `text` is role-prefixed multi-turn chunk content (`const line = `${t.role}: ${t.text}`.trim()`, line 255, joined by '\n\n', line 248).
- Direct MCP write passes NO hash (index.ts:1771-1778 forwards only agentId/kind/content/tags/taskId/project), so `effectiveHash = contentHash(content)` (swarmMemory.ts:546) = `sha256((content).normalize('NFC').replace(/\s+/g,' ').trim())` with no source/session prefix (swarmMemory.ts:526-529).
These differ by construction (source+sessionId prefix + un-normalized multi-turn text vs. bare NFC-collapsed line), so `seenHashes.has(effectiveHash)` is FALSE for a transcript predecessor — the finding's step 3 ("sees seenHashes.has(hash) is true") never fires, and the write is stored WITH project='foo'/tags=['tooling']. Scenario REFUTED as framed.

The defect IS reachable via a narrower, un-highlighted path: two byte-identical (post-NFC/whitespace) DIRECT writes where the earlier lacked/differed in project. Concretely reachable because the Electron IPC `memory:write` handler cannot even accept a project (index.ts:1090-1097 input type `{agentId; kind; content; tags?; taskId?}`, no project passed to memoryWrite), so a UI-written entry has no project; an agent later writing identical content via MCP with a project collides on contentHash and gets the project-less entry back. `memoryPatchProjects` (swarmMemory.ts:402-415) does NOT rescue this path: it is invoked only from ingestion pending-patches (conversationIngest.ts:358-360), not on the dedup return, only fills when `!e.project` (lines 405,412), and never unions tags/taskId.
verdict.notes: Severity corrected high->medium. The bug is genuine (silent metadata loss + hard-filtered project recall miss + agent misled by a success/id) but the finding overstates reachability: its lead trigger (transcript chunks the agent restates) cannot collide because ingestion uses a source+session-scoped sha256 over role-prefixed multi-turn text, distinct from the agent's contentHash of a bare line. The real trigger requires two exact-duplicate DIRECT writes with divergent/absent project (e.g. UI/IPC write with no project, then MCP write with one) — a real but bounded condition, not the broad path claimed. The proposed fix (backfill project when empty, union tags, adopt taskId on dedup hit, and/or return a deduped/mergedInto flag) is sound and would also close the direct-write path.

title: memory_anticipate fetches only `limit` semantic hits THEN filters to procedural/high-importance, so it returns an empty 'nothing known' whenever a stored lesson sits just below the fetch cutoff — defeating the anti-re-derivation tool
failureScenario: 1) The fleet earlier stored a procedural lesson 'Fix ELIFECYCLE on build by clearing node_modules/.cache' (memoryType:'procedural'). 2) Agent hits the error and calls memory_anticipate{task:'npm run build fails with ELIFECYCLE'}. 3) proactiveQuery extracts signals; memoryAnticipate calls memorySearch{query, limit: 5} (index.ts:1872) with diversify undefined → the plain top-5 by rank. Because the corpus also has many episodic transcript chunks mentioning 'build'/'ELIFECYCLE' that out-score the lone lesson on raw cosine+recency, the procedural lesson lands at rank 6. 4) Line 1873 filters the 5 fetched hits to memoryType==='procedural' || importance>=0.6; none of the top-5 qualify → returns []. The tool (whose contract is 'surface solutions the fleet has ALREADY found ... check it first, act second', mcpServer.ts:399-408) tells the agent nothing is known, so it re-derives a fix that already exists.
whyItMatters: This is the one tool explicitly sold as the re-derivation preventer, and its filter-after-fetch order turns a present lesson into a false negative. Worse, agent-written memories can't set importance (no schema field) so only reflection-authored lessons clear the 0.6 bar, making the top-5 window even more likely to exclude them.
proposedFix: Over-fetch then filter to limit: memorySearch({ query: q, limit: (opts.limit ?? 5) * 8 }) and slice the procedural/high-importance survivors to opts.limit; or push the memoryType/importance predicate into memorySearch as a filter so ranking happens over the eligible pool. Same fix pattern applies to any 'fetch N then post-filter' handler.

verdict.evidence:
The fetch-then-filter anti-pattern is REAL, but the finding's causal mechanism is factually wrong, making it narrower/less severe than claimed.

REAL PART — index.ts:1872-1873:
  const hits = await memorySearch({ query: q, limit: opts.limit ?? 5 })
  return hits.filter((h) => h.memoryType === 'procedural' || (h.importance ?? 0) >= 0.6)
No over-fetch; the non-diversify path is `survivors.slice(0, limit)` (swarmMemory.ts:1004-1006) with only a `score>0` gate (line 986), and `passesFilter` (swarmMemory.ts:784-790) does NOT exclude episodic chunks — so episodic chunks compete and a qualifying lesson at rank 6+ IS dropped → []. The proposed over-fetch-then-filter fix is sound.

WRONG PART — the finding claims "plain top-5 by rank" on "raw cosine+recency" with the lesson unaided. The actual ranking (swarmMemory.ts:983) is `learnedUtility(rankScore(...))`, which boosts exactly what the filter keeps:
- rankScore kindPriors (memoryEconomy.ts:98-122): {decision:1.15, fact:1.15}. A procedural lesson is written kind:'fact' (mnemeReflect.ts:188-189) → 1.15x. Auto-ingested episodic chunks are kind:'message' (conversationIngest.ts:465,495) → neutral 1.0x.
- learnedUtility importance nudge (mnemeRetrieval.ts:44-78): procedural lesson importance ≈0.7-0.95 (importanceFor, mnemeReflect.ts:133-139: 0.5 +0.2 procedural +0.15 success +entities) → +10.5-14.25%. Episodic chunks have no importance → no nudge.
- Net: at equal base relevance/recency the lesson out-multiplies a neutral episodic chunk by ~1.29x; BM25 length-normalization (swarmMemory.ts:962-963) further favors the short lesson on rare tokens like ELIFECYCLE. memoryType is explicitly "ORTHOGONAL to kind" (swarmMemory.ts:45), but procedural lessons still inherit the fact-kind prior.

So the ranking ACTIVELY floats procedural/high-importance lessons toward the top-5 — contradicting the "lands at rank 6" premise. Relegation is reachable only when episodic chunks have materially higher BASE relevance (e.g. a fresh burst of on-topic transcript chunks, recency ~1.25x, burying an old lesson), overcoming that ~1.29x advantage. The boosts are capped ("~+38%... never enough to lift a weak-but-nonzero hit past a strong one", mnemeRetrieval.ts:43), so it CAN happen but is not the default. Failure mode is a graceful false-negative (returns [] → agent falls back), not wrong output.
verdict.notes: Confirmed real: the fetch-N-then-post-filter with no over-fetch (index.ts:1872-1873) can return [] when a procedural/high-importance lesson sits below the limit=5 cutoff; no guard mitigates it in the non-diversify path, and the proposed over-fetch fix is correct. Downgraded from high to medium because the finding's reasoning is partly wrong: it treats ranking as raw cosine+recency, but rankScore gives the lesson's kind='fact' a 1.15 prior and learnedUtility adds a +~12% importance nudge (both verified against how procedural lessons are actually written), so the system already biases the top-5 toward exactly the memories the filter keeps. The "rank 6" scenario is thus far less likely than asserted and requires adversarial corpus conditions (recent, higher-base-relevance episodic chunks), and the impact is a graceful missed-recall, not incorrect output. Verdict PARTIAL.

title: memory_pool only pools the most-recent ~200 hot-window entries, which in any actively-ingesting brain are dominated by non-lesson transcript chunks — so it reports little/no cross-agent corroboration that in fact exists
failureScenario: 1) Over weeks, Claude and Codex each independently stored the lesson 'Always run migrations before seeding' (2-source corroboration). 2) The background indexer ingests transcript chunks every 90s (index.ts:1936-1943), each a kind:'message' entry with memoryType undefined, so the newest 200 inserted entries are almost all ingested messages. 3) Agent calls memory_pool. Handler does memoryList({limit:200}) — newest-first by insertion (swarmMemory.ts:1223-1229) — then .filter(m.memoryType==='semantic'||'procedural') (index.ts:1866). The two old lessons are far older than the 200 newest inserts, so they never enter the list; the filter yields few or zero lessons. 4) poolLessons returns [] or a thin set, so the tool (contract: 'Pool the shared brain's lessons across ALL agents ... the fleet's most-trusted, cross-validated knowledge', mcpServer.ts:388-397) tells the agent the fleet has no corroborated knowledge when it has plenty.
whyItMatters: The pool is presented as fleet-wide, cross-validated truth but is actually a keyhole onto the last few hundred inserts — and because ingestion constantly floods that window with messages, the durable distilled lessons are precisely what gets excluded. The agent under-trusts real corroboration.
proposedFix: Pool over lessons, not recency: select from the full hot window filtered to memoryType semantic/procedural (e.g., a dedicated iterator or memoryList variant that filters before applying the count cap), then cap. The `limit` should bound the number of LESSONS considered, not the number of raw recent rows scanned.

verdict.evidence:
Every link in the chain is present in the real code; no guard refutes it.

1) Handler caps RAW rows, then filters — index.ts:1864-1868:
  memoryPool: (opts) => poolLessons(
    memoryList({ limit: opts.limit ?? 200 })
      .filter((m) => m.memoryType === 'semantic' || m.memoryType === 'procedural')
      .map(...))
The cap (200) is applied to raw recent rows; the lesson filter runs AFTER.

2) memoryList is newest-first by insertion, has NO memoryType filter — swarmMemory.ts:1223-1229:
  const limit = Math.min(Math.max(opts.limit ?? 50, 1), 500)
  let pool = entries.slice().reverse()  // newest first
  ... return pool.slice(0, limit)
ListOptions (1216-1221) only offers limit/agentId/kind/since — no way to select lessons before the cap, and the row cap is hard-clamped at 500.

3) Ingested transcript chunks are non-lesson and land at the front — conversationIngest.ts:492-500 writes each chunk with `kind:'message'`, NO memoryType, NO ts. swarmMemory.ts:554 `ts: input.ts ?? Date.now()` (so even old transcripts get a fresh ingestion timestamp), :562 `...(input.memoryType && {memoryType})` (message chunks stay undefined → excluded by the raw filter), :582 `entries.push(stored)` (append order, so reverse() puts them first). inferMemoryType('message') → 'episodic' (mnemeTypeInfer.ts:61-62), a non-lesson, and the handler doesn't even call it — it reads raw m.memoryType.

4) The indexer continuously floods message chunks during active work — index.ts:1936-1943 fast tier every 90s ingests the active session (maxChunks 250); :1899-1907 full pass every 30 min (maxChunks 250). memoryWrite dedup returns the existing entry without refreshing ts (swarmMemory.ts:547-550), so recalled lessons are never bumped back into the recent window.

5) Real distilled lessons DO carry explicit semantic/procedural type, so they WOULD match the filter but for recency — mnemeReflect.ts:188 `memoryType:'procedural'`, :208 and :219 `memoryType:'semantic'`.

6) Documentary confirmation that untyped bulk entries dominate the store — mnemeTypeInfer.ts:5-9: "The store holds ~80k memories but almost none carry an explicit memoryType: only the Mneme reflection layer sets it ... The bulk code + transcript indexers — which authored the vast majority of entries — leave it undefined." Combined with maxEntries=500_000 (swarmMemory.ts:72), old lessons are NOT evicted — they simply sit far behind the newest 200 insertions.

7) The tool is live and singly-routed — mcpServer.ts:388-397 (contract: "Pool ... the fleet's most-trusted, cross-validated knowledge"); mcpServer.ts:531-532 dispatch to the one handler above. No alternate lesson-first pooling path exists.

Result: an agent calling memory_pool while a brain is actively ingesting gets poolLessons() computed over ~200 rows that are overwhelmingly kind:'message' episodic chunks; the semantic/procedural lessons written weeks earlier are far behind the recency cap and never enter the list, so corroboration that exists is under-reported. Reachable via the default (limit 200) and even at the API's hard max of 500 rows.

Severity stays medium (not higher): it silently degrades ONE advisory tool's contract at exactly the time it's used (active work), but there is no data corruption, and the store's other retrieval paths (memory_search / memory_anticipate) run over embeddings across the full store rather than the recency window, so cross-agent knowledge is still reachable by other means. The proposed fix (filter to lesson memoryType BEFORE applying the count cap — i.e. make `limit` bound lessons, not raw rows) is valid, since ListOptions currently cannot express a memoryType-filtered selection and the row cap is hard-clamped at 500.
verdict.notes: Secondary observation (not required for this verdict, but reinforces the fix): the handler filters on RAW m.memoryType while the dashboard uses inferMemoryType. A curated MCP `memory_write` note (kind:'note', no explicit memoryType) is treated as a 'semantic' lesson by inferMemoryType (mnemeTypeInfer.ts:48,63-64) yet is EXCLUDED by memory_pool's raw filter even when recent — so memory_pool under-counts curated notes independently of the recency issue. The finding's own scenario uses reflection-distilled lessons that DO carry explicit types, so it is unaffected by this caveat and remains fully valid.

title: memory_write 'max 16KB' silently truncates the tail of longer content and returns success — the conclusion of a long decision/architecture note is dropped with no signal
failureScenario: 1) Agent writes a 20KB architecture decision whose final paragraph is the actual ruling ('...therefore we will NOT adopt gRPC'). 2) memoryWrite hits line 537-539: content = input.content.slice(0, MAX_CONTENT) with MAX_CONTENT = 16*1024 (line 74). The last ~4KB — including the ruling — is discarded. 3) effectiveHash is computed over the TRUNCATED text (line 546), the truncated entry is stored and returned as a normal success. The tool description only says 'Text content to store (max 16KB)' (mcpServer.ts:269) with no statement that overflow is truncated rather than rejected. 4) Later recall returns the decision's setup without its conclusion; the agent confidently acts on a half-decision, and because the hash is of the truncated text, a corrected full re-write is treated as a DIFFERENT entry (no dedup), leaving both fragments in the store.
whyItMatters: Silent truncation is silent data loss at the exact boundary where long, high-value reasoning lives, and the agent is told the write succeeded. 'Never silently lose data' is violated for any content over 16KB.
proposedFix: Either reject content over MAX_CONTENT with a clear error the agent can react to (chunk-and-link), or return { truncated: true, storedChars, originalChars } so the caller knows. Update the tool description to state the exact overflow behavior. Prefer rejecting so the agent can split the note rather than losing its tail.

verdict.evidence:
The primary defect is real and reachable via the MCP memory_write tool; my attempt to find a guard failed.

WIRING (reachable): MCP memory_write dispatches at src/main/mcpServer.ts:475-483 `return await handlers.memoryWrite({...content: args.content...})` -> src/main/index.ts:1769 handler -> src/main/swarmMemory.ts:531 memoryWrite. No upstream size guard blocks 20KB: src/main/mcpServer.ts:711 `const MAX_BODY = 1024 * 1024 // 1MB limit` (413 only fires above 1MB, line 716-719); the inputSchema field at src/main/mcpServer.ts:269 `content: { type: 'string', description: 'Text content to store (max 16KB)' }` has NO maxLength; the IPC path src/main/index.ts:1090-1098 and the tool handler src/main/index.ts:1769-1778 pass content straight through. The only content guard is src/main/swarmMemory.ts:532 `if (!input || typeof input.content !== 'string' || !input.content.trim())` which rejects empty/non-string only.

DEFECT (swarmMemory.ts): line 74 `const MAX_CONTENT = 16 * 1024`; lines 537-539 `const content = input.content.length > MAX_CONTENT ? input.content.slice(0, MAX_CONTENT) : input.content` — slice(0, 16384) keeps the head and silently drops the TAIL (the finding's dropped conclusion). Line 546 `const effectiveHash = input.hash || contentHash(content)` hashes the TRUNCATED text. Line 557 stores `content` (truncated), line 574 `persist(entry)` writes the truncated copy to the durable JSONL too, and lines 579-582 return the entry with NO throw and NO truncated/storedChars/originalChars field. A repo-wide grep for `truncat`/`MAX_CONTENT` shows no truncation signal anywhere on this write path. At src/main/mcpServer.ts:580 the result is returned as a normal success (`result: { content: [...] }`, not isError). The tool description (mcpServer.ts:269) says only 'max 16KB', never disclosing that overflow is truncated rather than rejected. So: silent tail loss, success return, undisclosed contract — all confirmed.

WHERE THE FINDING OVERSTATES (step 4, dedup): an IDENTICAL 20KB re-write truncates to the same 16KB -> same hash -> `seenHashes.has(effectiveHash)` at swarmMemory.ts:547 is true -> it DEDUPS and returns the existing entry, contradicting the claim that a re-write is 'treated as a DIFFERENT entry (no dedup), leaving both fragments'. A genuinely corrected (different) note is legitimately a new entry in an append-only store, not a hashing bug. The actual hash-after-truncation hazard is the inverse and narrower: two DIFFERENT originals that share the same first 16KB collide into one entry (a false dedup that silently drops the second). This secondary framing is imprecise but does not weaken the core defect.
verdict.notes: Verdict CONFIRMED on the primary defect (silent tail truncation of >16KB content, returned as success, undisclosed in the tool contract, hash computed over truncated text) — fully reachable, no guard refutes it. Severity kept at medium: silent data-loss-on-success is a genuine contract violation and the tool is explicitly advertised for 'decisions, conventions, architecture/file notes' (mcpServer.ts:263), so losing a note's concluding ruling has real impact; but the 16KB cap (~16k chars) is generous so hit-frequency is low, and it is a local dev-tool memory brain. Note one weak, non-exculpatory mitigation: the returned entry echoes the truncated content back (serialized at mcpServer.ts:580), so a caller that diffed returned.content.length vs input length could in principle detect it — but nothing documents this and exactly-16384 chars is not self-evidently 'truncated', so 'no signal' is fair. The finding's step-4 dedup elaboration is misframed (identical re-writes DO dedup; the real risk is a false-dedup collision on shared 16KB prefixes) and should be corrected, but the core stands. Proposed fix is sound: reject over-cap content with a clear error (preferred, lets the agent chunk-and-link) or return {truncated,storedChars,originalChars}, and update the mcpServer.ts:269 description to state the exact overflow behavior.

title: memory_primer is headed 'most relevant first' but reorders conversation chunks ahead of higher-relevance decisions/facts and strips all timestamps — the leading item is neither most-relevant nor dated, so the agent can't tell an old chat from a current one
failureScenario: 1) For project 'foo', the gate yields a high-relevance decision D (score 0.82) and a low-relevance stale conversation chunk C (score 0.31, an old 'let's try X' musing that was abandoned). 2) buildContextPrimer's project bucket sort (lines 147-149) pushes all isConversation hits to the top regardless of score, so C is emitted BEFORE D. 3) The digest is wrapped with the header 'Relevant context from your memory (most relevant first)' (line 173), and renderLine (lines 82-93) emits '- [claude] <snippet>' with NO date/timestamp. 4) The agent, told the first line is the most relevant context, over-weights an abandoned idea and cannot distinguish a year-old conversation from yesterday's — there is no recency signal anywhere in the primer, even though each underlying entry has a ts.
whyItMatters: The primer is the first thing the agent 'holds' about a project. Labeling a conversation-first, recency-blind ordering as 'most relevant first' is a direct recency/relevance mislead, and without any date the agent cannot apply its own judgment about staleness. Combines with the superseded-not-filtered gap to make stale context lead the session.
proposedFix: Either change the header to match reality ('past conversations first, then most relevant') or drop the conversation-first reorder and sort purely by score. Add a compact relative-age marker to renderLine (e.g., '[claude · 8mo ago]') using the entry ts so the agent can weigh recency, and surface a 'superseded' marker for entries with a superseded-by edge.

verdict.evidence:
The mechanics are real (not a misread), but the harm is narrower and the "no recency anywhere" claim is overstated.

TRUE parts:
- Header, contextPrimer.ts:173 (unconditional, also shown in project branch): "Relevant context from your memory (most relevant first) — background only:"
- Conversation-first reorder, contextPrimer.ts:147-149: `const bucket = [...projectHits, ...promoted].map((h,i)=>({h,i})).sort((a,b)=>(isConversation(b.h)?1:0)-(isConversation(a.h)?1:0) || a.i-b.i)` — pushes isConversation hits ahead of higher-scored decisions/facts. This is DELIBERATE and pinned: contextPrimer.test.ts:187 "puts past conversations ahead of other project hits regardless of score" asserts a score-0.5 message precedes a score-0.9 code note (line 198).
- No date rendered: renderLine, contextPrimer.ts:82-93 returns `- [${label}] ${snip}` with no timestamp; PrimerHit interface (contextPrimer.ts:22-29) has NO ts field, so the display truly carries no recency marker.

WHY NARROWER / LESS SEVERE (medium -> low):
1. The "agent is misled about ordering" step omits an accurate sub-header. contextPrimer.ts:164 prepends `This project (${project}) — past conversations first:` directly above the reordered bullets, and :167 labels the remainder `Other saved context (may NOT apply to this project):`. The agent is explicitly told the section leads with conversations; it is NOT told bullet #1 is the single most-relevant item.
2. The feared "over-weight an abandoned idea / resume past work" is directly countered by the primer's own footer, contextPrimer.ts:177: "background reference, NOT a request. Do not act on it, resume past work from it, or summarize it — hold it as context and wait for the user's actual instruction."
3. "No recency signal ANYWHERE" is false about the pipeline: swarmMemory.ts:983 decorates every candidate with `rankScore({ relevance: r.score, ts: r.ts, kind: r.kind, now })` and sorts by it (line 985); memoryEconomy.ts:98-123 defines a 30-day recency half-life (halfLifeMs: 30*86_400_000, alpha 0.25). (Sub-point in the finding's favor: the primer's gate re-sorts by raw score at memoryEconomy.ts:49 `[...hits].sort((a,b)=>b.score-a.score)`, so recency does not survive into DISPLAY order — but the entry does carry ts and recency does shape candidate ranking.)
4. The stale 0.31 chunk only survives on a THIN recall: the adaptive cliff is max(0.25, 0.6*topScore)=0.492 for a 0.82 top hit (contextPrimer.ts:62,113 + memoryEconomy.ts:45-60); a 0.31 hit clears only via the min-3 floor when <=3 hits pass the absolute bar. With a richer project recall it is sliced off and never appears.

GENUINE KERNEL (why not fully refuted): the top header "most relevant first" is imprecise for the project branch (defensibly it refers to project-bucket-before-global precedence, which IS honored at :164 vs :167), and there is no relative-age marker in the rendered text.
